CodeRabbit scales agentic software development and ships 20x more

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (988 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.
  • It has been revealed that for Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a new window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work.
  • Sources indicate that codeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

CodeRabbit uses OpenAI models to govern and trust AI-generated code and Codex to ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team.

It has been revealed that for Harjot Gill, co-founder and CEO of CodeRabbit⁠(opens in a new window), trusting and validating agentic code is becoming the place where teams bring judgment to a growing volume of AI-generated work. “The first bottleneck that every tech giant hits as soon as you adopt coding agents is code reviews,” Harjot says.

Sources indicate that codeRabbit built an AI-powered governance and control platform designed to validate and trust AI-generated code. Used by over 20,000 organizations and 150,000+ open-source projects, CodeRabbit helps teams understand, review, and secure code produced by AI agents and decide what is ready to ship.

Industry observers note that according to CodeRabbit, better price-performance from OpenAI helps it add more AI agents to its reviews and pass the benefits to customers, and Codex⁠ helps it ship 20 times more software with the same engineering team. The organization also uses Daybreak⁠ to both secure its own stack and its customers’ code. Its latest offering, CodeRabbit Secure, uses Daybreak with Codex models to find and fix vulnerabilities using its security-focused agents.

According to recent reports, codeRabbit built its first product with GPT‑3.5 Turbo. Harjot states the arrival of GPT‑4 made the product effective at reviewing code. The organization went on to adopt OpenAI o1 and OpenAI o3 early. Because code reviews run asynchronously in the cloud, CodeRabbit could use models that took longer to reason through a problem in exchange for more capable analysis.

Industry observers note that the team evaluates new models against its own benchmark of known issues. At the time of the interview, Harjot estimated that GPT‑6 Astra⁠ caught 50% of the issues in that dataset, putting it at the top compared to other models in that benchmark.

It has been revealed that the benchmark continues to evolve as agents introduce different kinds of mistakes and as fixes reveal problems earlier reviews missed. “The nature of bugs keeps evolving, so does our benchmark as the models get better,” notes Harjot.

It has been revealed that better price-performance from OpenAI models has helped CodeRabbit move capabilities from research into its product. Harjot points to improvements in model pricing and caching that let the manufacturer use more AI, add more subagents, and pass the benefits to customers.

In a recent development, when CodeRabbit started, it used one or two subagents for code navigation. Lower-cost models such as GPT‑6 Luna now support more subagents throughout the platform, while models such as GPT‑6 Astra handle planning and orchestration.

Sources indicate that “Now we are using agents everywhere on the use cases we couldn't even afford in the past,” Harjot says. That expands the validation CodeRabbit can perform and the explanations it can give developers, helping them understand and trust changes they did not write themselves.

Sources indicate that by using Codex, Harjot claims the company has been shipping roughly 20 times more software over the last 6 months without adding engineers. He personally estimates that he pushed 2,500 to 3,000 pull requests in the 30 days before the interview.

According to recent reports, getting there required more than adopting Codex. Running multiple agents exposed constraints across the development process, from laptop memory and compute to testing, the tools that compile and package software, and dependencies.

Recent findings suggest that the team streamlined its release process and reconsidered where human approvals belonged, while using CodeRabbit to automatically ship low-risk changes that didn’t need human intervention. “We had to actually completely rethink the entire software delivery,” Harjot says.

It has been revealed that the organization has also built a Codex-powered Slack bot that triages production incidents, Slack messages, and support tickets. It can return a pull request for the team to review and merge. Harjot sees cloud-based development as a way to reduce local-machine constraints and give teams stronger controls over access and auditing.

According to recent reports, codeRabbit uses Codex for work beyond engineering, including managing marketing and operational tasks through code. “We are running the company as code as much as possible,” Harjot notes.

In marketing, the tech giant manages Google Ads through pull requests. The team opens and merges a request to deploy ads. It also uses a content studio repository where Codex creates slide decks and customer-facing documents. “If you can translate your marketing problems to code problems, you will run 10x faster,” Harjot claims.

CodeRabbit has run agents in sandbox environments since 2023, cloning repositories and letting agents write code to help perform reviews. More recently, CodeRabbit used OpenAI’s Cyber model through Daybreak to test and secure its own platform.

In a recent development, the team used the model for internal penetration testing, probing its own platform for ways an attacker could break in. Harjot notes the early access helped CodeRabbit secure its own stack. “We found multiple vulnerabilities, advanced hacks that we could not even imagine could happen,” Harjot says.

It has since taken those capabilities to market, helping secure its customers’ code with its latest product, CodeRabbit Secure. Over the past two weeks, the manufacturer ran a promotional offer where it covered $1M in free deep scans for their users and found over 43,000 security vulnerabilities across 13,000 deep scans, all powered by Codex models. Thousands of these vulnerabilities have already been fixed by its customers, helping improve their code security.

As background agents begin responding to alerts and incidents without a person initiating every task, Harjot expects teams to need more help deciding which changes to take to completion.

Looking ahead, CodeRabbit is expanding toward agentic software development, helping teams validate, prioritize, explain, secure, and verify agent-generated code changes at scale.

The opportunity is to help developers stay in control as agents do more of the building, with validation, explanations, and maintenance that keep pace with the code being produced.

  • This week at Slush, we are proud to highlight a remarkable group of European startups leveraging Google Cloud’s secure infrastructure and Gemini models to redefine their industries:.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

VP, Global Startups & Investor Ecosystem.

The front door to AI in the workplace.

As thousands of founders, investors, and technology leaders gather in Helsinki for Slush 2026, the European startup ecosystem is undergoing a profound transformation. The conversation has moved from  AI experiments to operating agents. Across Europe, the Middle East, and Africa (EMEA), pioneering startups are deploying autonomous AI agents that reason, integrate deeply with core systems, and automate complex workflows at scale.

At Google Cloud and Google DeepMind we’re focused on delivering a complete AI stack for startups,including; Gemini Enterprise and the Gemini agent; the industry’s broadest choice of proprietary models including Gemini, Claude, GPT; open models like Gemma; multiple compute options including both GPUs and TPUs;  the infrastructure required to build and scale AI applications; and the tools to manage huge volumes of data, monitor token spend, and more.

This week at Slush, we are proud to highlight a remarkable group of European startups leveraging Google Cloud’s secure infrastructure and Gemini models to redefine their industries:.

CDON (Sweden): As the largest e-commerce marketplace in the Nordics, CDON modernized its backend and data infrastructure on Google Cloud. Its analytics pipelines run on Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage, utilizing Python and FastAPI to ingest massive volumes of retail marketplace data. CDON democratizes real-time business reporting across brands and lays the groundwork for predictive personalization and generative AI workloads.

Sources indicate that chalkie.ai (UK):  A fast-growing education technology platform, Chalkie.ai uses Gemini's advanced reasoning capabilities to transform lesson planning for over 500,000 educators. By exporting directly to Google Slides Google Slides, teachers can instantly generate curriculum-aligned presentations and materials directly within their instructional tools while maintaining strict student data privacy standards.

Finova (UK): A leader in UK lending and savings software, has rolled out the UK’s first whole-of-market AI mortgage application agent, built on Google Cloud and Gemini. By deploying Gemini’s advanced reasoning to automate complex mortgage applications across multiple lender portals, Finova removes manual data entry bottlenecks and reduces errors. This saves mortgage brokers at least 30 minutes per application and reclaims thousands of operational hours industry-wide.

Sources indicate that fyndiq (Sweden): Swedish e-commerce marketplace Fyndiq (part of CDON Group) anchors its predictive analytics and data operations in Google BigQuery, dbt, and Google Cloud Storage. Fyndiq models transaction and product feed data to deliver near real-time business insights to merchandisers. By applying Google’s machine learning and performance models, Fyndiq optimizes customer acquisition and regional campaign reach.

Via Health Tech (Germany): Berlin-based VIA HealthTech is the AI assistant for psychotherapists. Powered by Gemini's multimodal audio and reasoning capabilities on Google Cloud, VIA turns therapy sessions into structured clinical notes within seconds and drafts psychological reports, giving therapists their time back for their patients. Trust is built in: VIA's security and compliance setup is BSI C5 attested and ISO 27001 certified, so therapists can use AI without compromising their professional secrecy. More than 4,000 clinicians already rely on it.

Building sustainable AI businesses requires infrastructure that combines high computational performance with strict data governance and predictable cost efficiency. This week we introduced the Google for Startups Accelerator: Sovereign AI (Europe & Israel). This equity-free, 12-week hybrid program is tailored for late-Seed to Series A startups handling high-stakes, regulated workloads across sectors like GovTech, HealthTech, and financial services. Participating founders receive 1:1 architectural mentorship from Google Cloud engineers, technical advisory support to prepare for EU AI Act regulatory sandboxes, and hands-on guidance deploying across our tiered sovereign portfolio—from the Google Cloud Data Boundary and partner-operated clouds like S3NS to air-gapped Google Distributed Cloud environments and open-weight models like Gemma.

Additionally, through the Google for Startups Cloud Program, startups across EMEA receive up to $350,000 in cloud credits , dedicated engineering support, and preferred access to partner tools and our AI infrastructure and models.

Whether you are building agents, scaling multi-modal applications, or migrating to scalable cloud infrastructure, Google Cloud provides the foundation for the next generation of EMEA startups .

If you are attending Slush 2026 in Helsinki, visit the Google Cloud booth to meet our engineering and startup teams, explore interactive demos, and learn more about applying to the Google for Startups Cloud Program.

Control Room: A central system to track and stop model workloads across our research infrastructure

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1272 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that as our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential concerns, and rapidly stop models in their tracks when needed.
  • Sources indicate that control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.
  • Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that as our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential concerns, and rapidly stop models in their tracks when needed. To solve this, we built Control Room.

Sources indicate that control Room is a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise. It connects every research inference workload, including agentic sampling for model training and evaluation, data processing, and more. This works together with our misalignment monitoring systems, and halts model output within 35 seconds of a decision to intervene to stop or pause a job. It has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.

Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest. Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to promptly take down model deployments if needed.

Control Room works by integrating a few systems: the workload, the inference engine, and the centralized Control Room service.

Recent findings suggest that the workload is the job being run, such as a reinforcement learning experiment, an evaluation, a high-volume sampling or data processing job. We require every research workload that does agentic inference to be associated with an approved safety case.

In a recent development, the inference engine, or just engine, is the model itself. You can think of the engine as the brain of the model, running directly on GPUs. A workload normally uses one or more models, which might be running on one or more different inference engines. The same inference engine might be used by more than one different workload.

The Control Room service tracks jobs and controls whether they are allowed to continue generating model output. Engines check with the Control Room service before fulfilling a request. If a job has been stopped, the service denies the request, preventing further output.

Control Room is integrated in the following way:.

When starting a latest job, the workload code requests a new job_id from Control Room.

Industry observers note that whenever the workload needs to sample tokens from a model, it makes a request to an inference engine running that model, passing the job_id. The engine requests permission from Control Room to fulfill that request, passing the job_id along to Control Room.

Control Room checks whether that job has been terminated, and if so, it denies the inference request. The engine responds to the workload's inference request with a refusal, stopping further model output from being produced for that job.

The process starts with a researcher launching a job—for example, an experiment or an evaluation.

Job code (or workload code) is owned and run by researchers. Inference engines might be started as part of this job, or standalone engines which are not associated with any particular job might already be running.

According to recent reports, the workload code requests a job ID, associating the job with an approved safety case. The job itself makes this request.

Control Room records the job and returns its identifier. The workload will attach this same ID to its inference requests.

The request includes the job_id. This request is made directly from the workload code and does not pass through Control Room.

Before fulfilling the request, the inference engine asks Control Room whether this job is still authorized to run.

Sources indicate that the job is still authorized, so Control Room grants permission. The inference engine can now fulfill the request.

The model generates a response and the engine sends it back to the research job. The job can use that output and continue its work.

It has been revealed that A person or monitoring system tells Control Room to stop this job. Control Room marks its ID as stopped. The workload code remains running.

We do not rely on the workload code to correctly perform a check of whether or not the job is still running.

The engine asks Control Room for permission to fulfill the fresh inference request, passing along the same job ID.

When the engine checks permission again, Control Room denies the stopped job. The engine must refuse the inference request.

The engine returns a refusal instead of model output. The research process may remain alive, and the engine remains available to other authorized jobs.

All of our frontier reinforcement learning jobs run with a monitor. A monitor is another model which inspects everything that the model-being-trained is doing, and raises an alert if it detects a problem. For example, our recent DNS-related incident⁠(opens in a latest window) was caught by a monitor.

Control Room and our monitoring system are integrated in the following way:.

If the monitoring system detects a potential issue, depending on the details and severity, the monitoring system may decide to stop the job.

In this case, the monitoring system sends a message to Control Room to stop the job, passing the job_id. Control Room records that the job is terminated.

Next time the job having that job_id makes an inference request to sample more tokens from any model running on any engine, the request will be denied, stopping further model output.

It has been revealed that the maximum time between the moment when Control Room receives an instruction to stop a job, and the moment when further progress is no longer possible, is 35 seconds. The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly.

According to recent reports, workloads, including experiments, evaluation jobs, etc., are normally owned and operated by researchers or teams of researchers. As a result, workload code changes often, and is not an ideal place to implement critical load-bearing safety protections. Because of this, our implementation is designed to be resilient to buggy or broken workload code.

We achieve this by implementing the termination mechanism in the inference layer. Workload code is highly-varied and decentralized. In contrast, there are only a very small number of inference code paths in use across all of OpenAI research, and their deployments are much more centralized and uniform. This means that the inference layer can serve as a bottleneck, where we can get strong guarantees that all model inference running in research is subject to Control Room authorization checks on every inference request. We additionally run continual agentic and programmatic sweeps to check that consumers are not accidentally or maliciously launching rogue engine implementations with Control Room unimplemented or disabled.

Finally, our system “fails closed”, meaning that the Control Room integration in the engines is configured in such a way that if the Control Room service goes down, either due to a system error or because it is disabled for any other reason, including tampering by a bad actor, then all inference requests will be denied until Control Room resumes normal operation. Fail-closed is rolled out now to all frontier model research workloads, and will finish rolling out across all remaining research workloads over the next few days.

Control Room is just one part of our holistic approach to safe frontier model training and deployment. We’ll continue to strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches. If you want to help build systems for the safe and secure development and deployment of AGI, we're⁠ hiring⁠!

Cogent and OpenAI build cyber defense factories for enterprises

📅 10 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (885 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.
  • Sources indicate that as Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them.
  • Industry observers note that cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cogent combines OpenAI models with enterprise context to help automatically remediate vulnerabilities with agents.

Lower mean time to remediate vulnerabilities.

Sources indicate that as Cogent Security⁠(opens in a new window) sees enterprises facing more security risks than ever, it has found that the hardest part is not finding vulnerabilities, but fixing them. Remediation work is complex and spans multiple teams. It requires contextual understanding of a company’s environment: how could an attacker exploit a vulnerability, which business systems are at stake, and what changes can be made safely.

Industry observers note that cogent builds Cyber Defense Factories for enterprises to autonomously find and eliminate those risks. The factories are designed to help defenders move at machine speed, in response to the acceleration in vulnerability discovery and exploitation.

According to recent reports, the manufacturer’s AI agents combine GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑5.6 with its enterprise context and controls to handle investigation through verified remediation. The agents assess exposures, execute permitted changes, and confirm the risk has been eliminated. Cogent also conducts internal research with Cyber and Daybreak, exploring attack paths and defensive capabilities.

Industry observers note that for each customer, Cogent’s Context Engine maintains an enterprise knowledge graph of assets, vulnerabilities, identities, ownership, and dependencies. Specialized background agents continuously reconcile information across security tools and systems, giving investigation and remediation agents a shared understanding of the environment.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 Astra handles upfront planning and complex reasoning for that work. This enables what Geng Sng, Co-founder and CTO of Cogent, describes as a “memory harness for the enterprise.” He says, “We don’t have to relearn what the world looks like every time a newly introduced task happens.” Reusing context reduces latency, inference costs, and inconsistent results.

According to recent reports, cogent’s Agent Policies define each enterprise’s permitted changes and approval requirements, and its policy-enforcement engine, TRACE, checks tool calls against the policies before execution. The checks are deterministic and require no separate model inference.

An Agent Gateway independently checks authorization, and higher-risk work can run in isolated sandboxes. Customers can delegate investigation, require approval for changes, or permit bounded autonomous remediation.

When critical security flaws known as PHP2Shell were disclosed in PHP, a programming language used to run websites, customers turned to the Cyber Defense Factories that Cogent had already deployed in their environments.

It has been revealed that GPT‑6.1 Sol and GPT‑6 Astra provided the deep reasoning for investigation and remediation planning. Using Cogent’s context layer, agents identified affected systems, assessed exposure, and developed plans that accounted for application dependencies and operational constraints. Then they orchestrated fixes using customer-defined approval and execution workflows and verified the resolution.

Cogent reports that customers are using its Cyber Defense Factories to resolve vulnerabilities faster and expand investigation capacity. With Cogent, a Fortune 1000 automotive customer reduced its mean time to remediate critical vulnerabilities by 75%, and a Fortune 500 IT services customer achieved 5× vulnerability-triage throughput.

It has been revealed that global electronic trading platform MarketAxess leverages Cogent to help strengthen its risk-based approach to exposure management. “Cogent brings together vulnerability data, business context, security controls, and attack path analysis to help us validate real exposures and prioritize remediation where it matters most. What stands out is how rapidly the Cogent team responds to emerging threats and turns our feedback into practical capabilities,” says Vijay Bala, CISO, MarketAxess.

Recent findings suggest that cogent continuously evaluates closed-source and open-source alternatives and reports stronger reasoning on long-running security tasks, higher fidelity, fewer hallucinations on technical codebases, and more reliable execution with OpenAI models. The models can chain tool calls sequentially and in parallel while retaining context across remediation workflows.

Sources indicate that cogent prioritizes reasoning quality for complex investigations and cost for more straightforward work. It uses GPT‑6.1 Sol for general execution and GPT‑5.6 for routine vulnerability-management tasks where advanced reasoning is less critical.

In a recent development, using OpenAI models has also reduced the supporting software Cogent needs to build for remediation and patching. “A lot of the work that we had to do at the harness level is no longer required,” Geng claims. He also shared that OpenAI APIs have “streamlined request routing and agent orchestration, significantly reducing internal engineering overhead and accelerating our time-to-market for complex security workflows.”.

Industry observers note that most of Cogent’s engineers also choose Codex for development. Geng says they’re more productive pairing Codex with OpenAI models vs. using the same models in an open-source coding environment. “Codex just comes with tools that we don’t have to build ourselves,” says Geng.

Industry observers note that through Trusted Access for Cyber and Daybreak, Cogent receives technical support for its internal red-teaming and attack-path research. Daybreak Red, an access tier within Daybreak, provides the team with specialized OpenAI models for authorized offensive and vulnerability research. “Good defense requires good offense,” Geng says.

Cogent prepares to expand its capabilities as the key partner for enterprises to build their own Cyber Defense Factories. Its roadmap includes increasingly autonomous remediation, broadening the range and complexity of fixes agents can execute, from straightforward configuration changes to multi-step workflows spanning different enterprise systems.

The company is also developing autonomous discovery and validation. Its goal is a closed-loop system that finds and eliminates risk while continuously learning from every vulnerability to improve future investigations and fixes.

Latest Update: Work at the Frontier: AI’s effect on freelance work

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Upcoming research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.
  • For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a fresh skill or expands a project’s scope.
  • Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a upcoming window) found that 38% of skilled U.S.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Upcoming research from OpenAI and Upwork finds shifting demand for freelance services, new combinations of skills, and larger budgets for AI-related projects.

For freelancers, changes in the market arrive one assignment at a time: a client needs a different service, requests a fresh skill or expands a project’s scope. Our new research with Upwork offers an early view of these changes in the AI era. Some familiar services are losing market share, while AI-related projects bring together different capabilities—and involve larger budgets and more hours of work.

The stakes are substantial. Upwork’s 2026 Future Workforce Index⁠(opens in a upcoming window) found that 38% of skilled U.S. knowledge workers freelance. Its previous annual study⁠(opens in a new window) estimated that freelance knowledge work generated $1.5 trillion in U.S. earnings in 2024. Those estimates extend well beyond Upwork’s own marketplace.

Recent findings suggest that freelance work can also reveal changes sooner than economy-wide employment statistics. Contracts are often short, and clients can adjust their requirements with each posting. To get to the root of these changes, we partnered with Upwork, an online marketplace connecting clients and freelancers, to study those requests alongside the activities people undertake directly with ChatGPT.

The mix of work differed across the two platforms. Writing accounted for a much larger share of ChatGPT use, while video and animation accounted for larger shares of requests for freelancers in Upwork postings.

Below are the ranges of tasks between the two platforms.

According to recent reports, these activities represent only the largest changes in Upwork shares over the studied period. ChatGPT shares cover Jan 2025–Jun 2026; Upwork shares are H1 2026. Changes in Upwork share are H1 2025 to H1 2026, in percentage points.

Many activities that were relatively common in ChatGPT lost share on Upwork, while less common activities gained share. Of the 63 work categories analyzed, 43 followed this pattern.

The remaining 20 work categories revealed the reverse. ChatGPT use alone does not explain changes in freelance demand.

The comparison also captures how people currently use ChatGPT, not the full range of tasks AI can support—a gap OpenAI calls the capability overhang.

Each point represents one of 63 matched work subcategories in the Upwork taxonomy. The horizontal axis is the natural log of the category’s share of ChatGPT use in H2 2025 divided by its share of Upwork job posts in H1 2023. The vertical axis indicates the percentage change in the category’s share of Upwork postings from H1 2023 to H2 2025, on a logarithmic scale; 0% indicates unchanged marketplace share. The vertical divider at AI intensity 0 marks equal category shares in ChatGPT and baseline Upwork postings.

By late 2025, clients were requesting the use of AI in many more, different kinds of work. Clients were seeking freelancers to apply AI in tasks including chatbot development, video production, marketing automation, and application integration.

Within individual projects, AI capabilities were often requested alongside other work. AI-related postings listed about as many tasks as other postings but more often combined tasks that had rarely appeared together in earlier jobs.

Industry observers note that some clients asked for AI-generated video, editing, and motion graphics in a single posting. The freelancer would bring those skills together to deliver a finished video.

Between early 2023 and late 2025, the mix of tasks in AI-related postings became 45% more diverse—the equivalent of an increase from about 15 equally common tasks to about 21.

Although posted hourly rates were similar for AI-related and other work, AI-related projects had larger fixed-price budgets and involved more hours of work. This pattern suggests that higher budgets may partly reflect a broader scope of work.

AI’s effects on work can be difficult to detect in employment statistics. As we have noted in previous Work at the Frontier papers, the effects may appear first in the work people do.

Because freelance projects turn over rapidly, postings are continually refreshed as clients’ needs change. Work within firms can evolve without appearing in a upcoming job posting. Combined with ChatGPT data, these postings offer an early view of which activities people undertake directly with AI, which they hire freelancers to perform, and how AI-related projects differ from other work.

The findings do not point to a simple substitution story. Some activities common in ChatGPT use lost share on Upwork, but this pattern was not uniform. AI-related work also spanned a wider mix of activities, combined tasks in less familiar ways, and carried larger fixed-price budgets and more hours. Together, these patterns suggest that AI may be shifting both what clients seek from freelancers and how they assemble projects.

The OpenAI Economic Research Team explores how AI is changing work in real time with the Work at the Frontier series.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With the OpenAI API and models, Singapore Airlines improves customer support, travel discovery, and employee work, doubling CSAT for the Kris customer service chatbot.

Increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT) with AI-powered Kris chatbot.

Reduction in average handling time for customer service representatives using AI-assisted tools.

Growth in Flight Recommender monthly owners over the past year.

Sources indicate that AI is becoming part of how Singapore Airlines serves customers, empowers employees, and builds technology. The airline uses the OpenAI API for customer-facing experiences and OpenAI models inside Jarvis, its governed internal AI platform for employees. It also uses OpenAI models in its software development workflows to deliver more personalized service, improve productivity, and help teams build more efficiently.

Across these deployments, Singapore Airlines pairs OpenAI models with orchestration, internal data controls, validation, and human review, giving teams a consistent way to bring AI into production workflows responsibly.

It has been revealed that one of Singapore Airlines’ most visible AI applications is Kris, its customer-facing chatbot. After moving Kris from a traditional dialog-flow system to an LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API, Singapore Airlines saw a 2x increase in customer satisfaction.

Industry observers note that alongside that, the airline deployed AI-assisted tools for customer service representatives, including OpenAI API-powered call summarization, so that representatives spend less time on after-call work and more time on the customer. Singapore Airlines saw an approximately 10% reduction in average handling time for its customer service representatives.

In the earlier dialog-flow based chatbot design, every topic had to be mapped manually, and every flow had to be written in advance. That made coverage difficult to scale. If an intent was missing, the conversation was more likely to end up requiring support from a customer service representative, even when the customer’s request could have been handled through self-service.

Recent findings suggest that singapore Airlines moved Kris to a fully LLM-powered conversational experience using the OpenAI API. Instead of depending on predefined flows, the chatbot can interpret customer intent in natural language, ground answers in a knowledge base, manage multi-topic conversations, and hand over to a customer service representative with the relevant context when needed.

It has been revealed that today, customers use Kris for general queries, special requests, real-time flight disruption information, and selected transactional workflows. Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand its capabilities to include booking changes, baggage transactions, and more complex agentic interactions.

Flight Recommender lets customers describe the trip they want in natural language instead of repeatedly adjusting filters, dates, and destinations. Usage has grown nearly 3x over the past year.

Built on the OpenAI API, Flight Recommender uses an orchestration layer connected to fare and availability data. It interprets customer intent, calls the relevant tools, and returns personalized travel recommendations in natural language.

The team has also implemented guardrails for input and output validation, malicious or inappropriate query handling, hallucination reduction, PII handling, and authenticated access to only the context required for each query. Singapore Airlines is preparing to expand the experience into a more conversational chatbot interaction, where customers can keep refining travel ideas rather than restarting a search.

Beyond customer-facing experiences, Singapore Airlines is also using OpenAI models in parts of the software development lifecycle to help teams blueprint, refine, test, and review work more efficiently. Across selected software development lifecycle activities, teams have achieved productivity gains of up to 20%.

AI now runs through the entire delivery lifecycle and not just coding. Teams use generative AI models to support requirements refinement, stakeholder-session analysis, product specifications, edge-case identification, test-case creation, architecture review, and the breakdown of complex work into smaller, more testable tasks.

For one commercial feature, the team used the OpenAI API to challenge assumptions, identify ambiguous requirements and surface edge cases before development begins. Once those were well-defined, AI helped translate them into design options, implementation prepares, test cases and then code generation.

Industry observers note that during deployment and beyond, AI also helps to interpret how the system is behaving in production, and flagging issues that might otherwise go unnoticed. With AI active at every step of the workflow, team members have shifted from producing every artifact themselves, to directing, reviewing and validating what AI produces throughout the delivery lifecycle. This means they can focus on work that truly requires human judgement, such as prioritization, architecture, governance and stakeholder outcomes.

In a recent development, more broadly, OpenAI models are helping Singapore Airlines improve requirements quality, test coverage, and conformance with internal standards. Teams use these workflows to generate edge cases for testing, review architecture plans, and support human validation before work moves further through the development lifecycle.

In a recent development, beyond engineering teams, Singapore Airlines is making AI accessible across the business through Jarvis, its internal AI platform. Powered by OpenAI models, Jarvis gives employees a governed way to use AI in their day-to-day work, from summarizing documents to creating custom workflows.

Employees use Jarvis to work across PDFs, Word documents, Excel files, PowerPoint decks, and other file types in a secure environment, while creating custom workflows and lightweight knowledge bases for their day-to-day work. Today, more than 60% of Singapore Airlines employees are using Jarvis monthly with adoption continuing to increase.

2x increase in customer satisfaction score (CSAT) after changing to AI-based Kris chatbot.

~10% reduction in average handling time for customer service agents using AI-assisted tools.

3x growth in monthly users of Flight Recommender, its customer-facing travel discovery tool, over the past year.

Singapore Airlines is continuing to expand AI across customer and employee workflows. For Kris, the next phase is deeper self-service, with more transactional capabilities that help customers resolve requests directly in chat. Flight Recommender is moving toward a more conversational travel discovery experience, where customers can refine ideas over multiple turns rather than restarting a search.

It has been revealed that with Jarvis available across the business, Singapore Airlines is focused on helping more employees put AI to work in their day-to-day roles. Together with its customer-facing innovations, this is helping the airline build a future where AI makes travel more seamless, employees more productive, and the business more responsive to changing needs.

Industry News: Closing the AI guidance gap in education

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Drawing on fresh ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.
  • Industry observers note that AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for.
  • Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Drawing on fresh ThinkYoung research and lessons from our EMEA partnerships to support independent learning with AI.

Industry observers note that AI is prompting a fundamental reassessment of what education should prepare societies for. As intelligence becomes easier to access and apply, the question is no longer simply what people need to know, but which skills and capabilities will help them thrive in an AI-enabled world. Recent debates around PISA and AI, including those led by the OECD’s Andreas Schleicher⁠(opens in a upcoming window), underscore this shift. They also point to a central lesson: as AI becomes more capable, the role of teachers becomes more important, not less. Their expertise, judgement and ability to guide learning remain essential. Equipping teachers, schools and governments with AI skills and confidence to make informed decisions about these tools must therefore be a priority for education systems.

Across EMEA, we are working with governments and education systems, including in Estonia, Slovakia, Greece and Italy, amongst others to explore how AI can support educators. These collaborations share three priorities: equitable access to frontier AI tools, jointly designed AI literacy programmes, and ongoing measurement and evaluation, whilst adapting to local languages, curricula and institutions.

This report shares emerging lessons from our education partnerships in EMEA, focusing on educator support, AI literacy, local capability and evaluation. It examines what partners have tried, what they have reported and what remains uncertain. Country examples reflect their particular contexts and arrangements, and their findings should be interpreted within those limits. Five themes organise these lessons: clear educational goals, educator preparation, local partnerships, critical AI literacy and credible evidence.

Three early patterns are emerging from this work:.

Country partnerships offer context-specific lessons. Experiences in Estonia, Greece and Slovakia point to three lessons that other education systems can apply: strong public leadership to set a clear direction, investment in teachers' skills and confidence, and practical support tailored to local curricula and classroom needs. While implementation will vary across countries, these principles offer a useful foundation for governments seeking to integrate AI responsibly and at scale.

Closing the AI guidance gap in education is becoming increasingly urgent. Newly introduced research from ThinkYoung,⁠(opens in a new window) which examines the ways teachers and students are already engaging with AI highlights a clear guidance gap: 79% of surveyed students reported using AI for homework or assignments, but only 47% reported being shown how. Governments need to support educators and give students clearer expectations. Below we set out how educators can be better supported to set the terms and conditions of use.

Early benefits for teachers are clear. Adoption and reported time savings for teachers are encouraging. Understanding where AI strengthens knowledge, independent thinking and retention requires sustained evaluation and through the government actions that we observed, we identify how to prioritise more research into this critical area.

Our aim is to share practical lessons from these partnerships that education leaders can consider in their own contexts. These are early experiences, rather than a single model for education systems to follow.

In a recent development, we are also learning how to judge progress with evidence: teacher adoption and reported time savings offer encouraging early signals. Surveys, programme monitoring and consultation help us understand participants’ experiences and the barriers they encounter.

Sources indicate that at OpenAI, our mission is to ensure that artificial general intelligence benefits everyone. Helping learners flourish is central to that ambition. We believe that every young person should have the opportunity to develop the skills to participate in a world increasingly shaped by AI, whatever their background or wherever they attend school. We have a responsibility to contribute to that evidence and learn openly from the findings, including when they challenge our assumptions. Through the OpenAI Learning Lab, we are bringing education researchers together to understand when and how AI can support education systems.

It has been revealed that the choices made today will shape how the next generation learns, works and participates in society. With ambition, care, public leadership and a commitment to evidence, AI can help extend educational opportunity and strengthen young people’s capacity to understand, create and act for themselves.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • We’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a new way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week.
  • Recent findings suggest that together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Claim your business, keep your information current, and understand how people engage with you in ChatGPT.

We’re introducing Businesses in ChatGPT in beta, giving businesses a new way to connect with the 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT each week. Through Business Hub⁠(opens in a new window), businesses can claim their business, manage their information, and see insights on how people engage with them on ChatGPT. In addition, we are adding a powerful new way for businesses to interact with customers via Business Agents, starting with eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the U.S.

Recent findings suggest that together, these products create more ways for businesses to connect with people as they explore options and make decisions. They strengthen how people discover and interact with businesses in ChatGPT through broader business coverage, up-to-date information, and the ability to connect with a business through its Business Agent. Throughout these experiences, protecting the trust people place in ChatGPT remains our North Star.

Recent findings suggest that in Business Hub, companies can claim their organization in ChatGPT and, once verified, revision key details and add self-service product feeds with pricing and availability. This gives businesses a new way to provide information to ChatGPT, helping people explore products and services using the most accurate and up-to-date details.

Recent findings suggest that any eligible business located where ChatGPT is available can claim their business in ChatGPT through Business Hub. Existing OpenAI Enterprise customers and advertisers can work directly with their OpenAI representative to claim their business. Shopify merchants can connect their store from Business Hub or the Shopify admin to streamline verification. Eligible products from Shopify merchants are already integrated into ChatGPT through Shopify Catalog.

According to recent reports, business Hub provides aggregated insights into how people engage with a business in ChatGPT. This includes the number of mentions and website clicks a business receives. Businesses can also explore discovery topics—common themes across conversations where their website is cited. These insights can help businesses understand how they’re represented and find opportunities to improve the information they share.

It has been revealed that we’ve designed these insights to protect user privacy. We don’t share consumers’ conversations or Business Agent chats with businesses. Insights are aggregated and are only available when there are enough conversations or interactions to meet certain thresholds.

After claiming their business in ChatGPT, eligible organizations can build, test, and launch a Business Agent—a new way to answer questions and help people explore their offerings.

According to recent reports, when a business appears in a model response, people can click to see the business’s ChatGPT profile. If a Business Agent is available, customers can choose to start a conversation with the business to explore its offerings and ask follow-up questions. For example, someone comparing products could ask about the differences between two options and which features fit their needs. A Business Agent could help them explore those questions using the business’s information.

For customers, this can make it easier to understand whether an offering is the right fit. For businesses, it creates a way to help interested customers learn more through a personalized conversation. The Business Agent conversation is clearly labeled, separate from the customer’s original ChatGPT conversation, and distinct from ChatGPT’s independent answers.

According to recent reports, businesses can also sponsor their Business Agent⁠ and use it as the destination for ChatGPT Ads to reach more potential customers. Sponsored placements are clearly labeled and separate from ChatGPT responses.

In a recent development, business Agents are now available to eligible ecommerce and online service businesses in the United States. Learn more about eligible categories here⁠.

Sources indicate that as people turn to AI to discover products, compare options and make decisions, ChatGPT has become the platform for people and businesses to connect through AI. Today’s announcement is an early step in bringing businesses more deeply into ChatGPT. We’re starting with the foundations: accurate business information, useful insights, and conversations that help people make informed decisions. Over time, we strategy to expand Businesses in ChatGPT and Business Agents to more markets and business categories, and build tools for organizations with more complex needs.

As the platform evolves, we’ll explore more ways for businesses to connect with customers—directly or through agents—in ChatGPT and beyond. Our goal is to make ChatGPT more useful for people making decisions, and give businesses fresh ways to participate and grow.

Learn more and⁠ claim your business in ChatGPT.⁠.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, bringing free, hands-on ChatGPT workshops to five U.S. cities during National Family Caregivers Month.

Caregiving often means juggling schedules, keeping track of information, and finding support while balancing work and family life. During National Family Caregivers Month, we’re helping caregivers gain AI skills that can make some of those everyday tasks easier, giving them more time to focus on the people they care for.

According to recent reports, on November 10, OpenAI Academy, in collaboration with Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, and American Diabetes Association®, is hosting the AI Skills Jam for Caregivers & Community Health: a free, in-person learning experience designed to help caregivers use ChatGPT confidently, safely, and practically. These nationwide events will bring together participants across five U.S. cities, including individual and family caregivers, caregiver support organizations, and people living with chronic or serious health conditions:.

According to recent reports, an OpenAI analysis estimates that more than 40 million weekly ChatGPT messages about healthcare in the U.S. ask about healthcare for someone else1. At the workshops, participants will explore how ChatGPT can help with resource navigation, peer support, and caregiver support, including how to:.

organize caregiver schedules and checklists.

turn trusted educational resources into plain-language materials.

prepare support group discussion guides.

Participants will also learn how to use AI responsibly, including protecting personal information and understanding the limits of these tools. Participants will also learn when to consult healthcare professionals and how AI tools should complement, not replace, medical, legal, or financial advice. OpenAI facilitators and mentors will offer hands-on support throughout the workshops. No coding or technical background is required.

According to recent reports, the Jam brings this learning into local communities, where caregivers can practice alongside peers and share the everyday challenges they hope these tools can help address. Our partners bring deep expertise and experience supporting people living with serious illness and their families. Their perspectives, together with those of caregivers themselves, will help connect the day’s learning to the needs of each community.

Industry observers note that the AI Skills Jam is part of OpenAI Academy’s broader work to make AI practical and accessible to everyone. It builds on previous events we’ve hosted with nonprofits, small businesses, K–12 educators, and older adults.

Recent findings suggest that we are grateful to Caregiver Action Network, Alzheimer’s Association, American Diabetes Association®, and the caregivers and community health organizations joining us across the country. Their questions, ideas, and experiences will help shape future learning resources and ensure these tools are useful in the daily work of supporting others.

This is from a privacy-preserving ChatGPT usage estimate for October 9–29, 2026.

JioStar’s chief architect on AI discovery at 500M-user scale

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (896 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A conversation with Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect at JioStar.
  • Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.
  • It has been revealed that jioStar operates entertainment and live-sports platforms used by more than 500 million consumers and has supported as many as 72.5 million concurrent live-sports viewers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A conversation with Vijay Seshadri, Chief Architect at JioStar.

Our Executive Function series features perspectives from leaders driving transformation through AI.

It has been revealed that jioStar operates entertainment and live-sports platforms used by more than 500 million consumers and has supported as many as 72.5 million concurrent live-sports viewers. At that scale, AI has to be fast, reliable, and ready for production.

In a recent development, using the OpenAI API, JioStar built a conversational video and cricket-stat discovery assistant into JioHotstar. Viewers can speak naturally to find movies and shows, historical highlights, live-match moments, or cricket statistics, with results returned through a visual, conversational experience.

At OpenAI’s Executive Summit in Singapore, Sidharth Sharma, OpenAI’s Head of Go-to-Market for ASEAN, spoke with Vijay Seshadri—Chief Architect, JioStar, about building the experience for more than 15 languages in about eight weeks, and the lessons for leaders taking AI from demo to production.

According to recent reports, content discovery has evolved very little in the past 25 years. Recommendations were the last major shift. Much of what followed has been an iteration of the same idea.

In a recent development, but choosing what to watch is deeply personal. A person might say, “I’m feeling sad. Show me something that will cheer me up.” Even that simple request contains a lot of nuance. What kind of sad? What usually cheers that person up? Do they want comedy, comfort viewing or something completely distracting?

A traditional recommendation system may struggle to understand that moment. Conversation gives the viewer a way to explain it. We call this a voice-visual interface.

We began working through the concept in October and November, with a major cricket tournament coming in February. We had roughly two months and two very different audiences: entertainment viewers and cricket fans.

An entertainment viewer might say, “It’s Friday evening—surprise me,” or describe a movie without knowing its title. Sports viewers may want a more specific update, like fall of wickets, a series of sixes, or the match in which a player scored a certain number of runs. Cricket experts may want statistics about every ball.

It has been revealed that these are very different discovery problems. We worked on bringing entertainment, sports moments and detailed cricket statistics into one experience, across multiple languages, in a very short period.

Recent findings suggest that very early, we framed the problem as a three-way tradeoff among accuracy, latency, and cost. Every engineering decision had to balance all three at once.

Voice made that especially important. More than 60% of our customers use voice rather than text: people prefer to say what they want to watch. The response still has to be relevant, fast, and economically viable at scale.

Sources indicate that I think about it in two parts: an evaluation framework and a validation layer. Before production, the evaluation framework should prompt changes. In production, a feedback loop should turn customer behavior and failures into new eval cases.

That flywheel can become self-amplified, but it is extremely difficult to get right.

Domain experts are essential. For sports-statistics evals, we worked with people such as sports-magazine editors who understood what serious fans might ask. You cannot begin with a prompt alone; you need to seed the system with deep human expertise.

Industry observers note that one thing we got right was the team. We started with a small team of data scientists and engineers around a clear problem statement. OpenAI’s forward-deployed engineers worked alongside us to further identify the few things we absolutely had to get right.

The first was scope. A voice or text interface lets users ask almost anything, so we began by deciding what the system should not answer. Guardrails came first.

For evals, we began with a seed dataset and used models to expand it with more variation. We created what you might now call a maker-checker pattern: one model helped determine how to answer a question, while another acted as a validator—an LLM as judge—with a competing objective.

Sources indicate that that raised another question: who tests the judge? Designing the validator was itself an evaluation problem. Codex helped the team accelerate work such as generating eval cases and updating the system, but faster building did not remove the need for judgment and validation.

I would invest earlier in production monitoring for model efficacy.

Traditional infrastructure measures such as P99 latency remain vital, but they are not enough. You also need to monitor model efficacy in production.

First, there is a large gap between what technology can do and the reality inside an enterprise. If your firm has not matched every frontier-model announcement, you are not alone.

Second, keep focusing on outcomes rather than activity. It is easy to mistake visible motion for meaningful progress, particularly when companies emphasize input metrics. Lines of code generated, for example, do not tell you whether you created meaningful value.

Finally, most enterprises underestimate the human skill and agency required. This cannot be only a generic skilling program. Leaders need people who can apply these tools with judgment. Give a strong engineer a tool like Codex and the impact can multiply; without the judgment to validate production systems, the risk multiplies too.

You have a rocket in your hands. Especially in production systems, you need validation and guardrails, and you need to give the keys to the right people.
