Qwen3.8 27B (118 calls, 1.9M tokens).

Build a Pac-Man-style game in Godot and leave it running.

A rectangular maze of walls laid out on a grid, with pellets filling every open corridor. A player marker moves continuously along the corridors, eating each pellet it passes over and scoring a point for it. Three ghosts move through the same corridors and chase the player. If a ghost catches the player, the player loses a life and everything resets to its starting position. Score and lives are drawn on screen.

No one is going to play this. The player drives itself with a simple heuristic: at each junction it heads toward the nearest pellet, unless a ghost is close, in which case it moves away from the ghost. The game must run unattended and indefinitely, with no keyboard input at all.

When it works, start the game and leave it playing.

Holo4 27B (68 calls, 2.4M tokens, 268 lines).

Qwen3.8 27B (197 calls, 11.4M tokens, 327 lines).

It has been revealed that our internal set of agentic pipelines builds interactive environments and verifiable tasks from documentation alone, such as screenshots of real websites or open-source software. So far it has produced about 10,000 tasks across web apps, MCP servers and desktop environments, including hybrid environments that expose the same state through a GUI and MCP.

Recent findings suggest that alongside training, we rebuilt our harness, the loop that executes the model's actions and manages its context over hundreds of steps, using feedback from agentic performance on OSWorld 2.0. Agents tagged why each task failed and engineers reviewed their fixes. The largest changes were giving the agent a reliable memory that can keep track of hundreds of steps, and a shell on the desktop machine itself.

Sources indicate that opus 5 (70.2%) and GPT-5.6 Sol (66.2%) use max-effort partial rewards on the v2026.08.08 offline set from OpenAI's launch chart, as in the cost-performance plot. Other reference scores come from model cards and the official leaderboard. Task releases, subsets and harnesses vary.

Sources indicate that our post-training stack is designed to adapt to new foundation models and produce agents that generalize across interfaces and environments. As a member of the NVIDIA Nemotron Coalition, we applied our latest stack to the Nemotron 3 Nano Omni model as a follow-up to Holotron 3.

The same recipe turns Nemotron 3 Nano Omni into Holotron4 Nano, a generalist agentic model that significantly improves over the base model on GUI workflows and in environments exposing MCP, APIs or coding sandboxes.

Gains are absolute percentage-point improvements over Nemotron 3 Nano Omni.

These gains show that our recipe transfers well and can turn a generalist model into an agentic expert. Nothing in it is size-specific.

In a recent development, both sizes are available today on the H Models API. Weights are on Hugging Face in BF16, FP8, NVFP4 and 4-bit GGUF, next to our small model, Holotron4 Nano.

We will release optimized DSpark drafter checkpoints in the coming days to further accelerate inference.

#20431. Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1817 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Getting the Source Right, Not Just the Fact: Source-Aware Verification for MCP Agents

📅 29 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1817 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage.
  • Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap.
  • In a recent development, consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this proposal includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Tool-using LLM agents no longer read from a single retrieved passage. Through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), an agent can call a search tool, inspect a structured patient or account record, query a database, and pull metadata, then weave all of it into one answer. That m aakes the usual question of factuality more subtle than it looks. Most of the systems built to check LLM answers, from RAGAS faithfulness to fine-grained checkers like MiniCheck, AlignScore, and SummaC, ask whether a claim is supported by the available evidence once that evidence has been pooled together. In their usual form, they do not tell us which MCP tool output supports each claim, or whether that is the source the answer names.

Our latest paper, ProvenanceGuard: Source-Aware Factuality Verification for MCP-Based LLM Agents (read it on Hugging Face, or on arXiv in the meantime), targets that gap. The failure mode we care about is one we call cross-source conflation: a claim that is true somewhere in the evidence, but attributed to the wrong source. A source-blind verifier may pass it, because the fact does exist in the pool. A source-aware verifier should not.

In a recent development, consider a customer support agent that answers, "According to the account record, this proposal includes a 30-day refund window." The refund window may be perfectly real, but stated in a policy document, not in the account record the answer points to. Pool the two together and the claim looks supported. Keep them separate and the attribution is wrong, and in a data-sensitive setting a wrong attribution can be as damaging as a wrong fact. The same pattern shows up in a clinical agent, where a patient-specific medication detail taken from a patient-history tool becomes misleading the moment the answer presents it as a finding from the medical literature.

A claim can be supported by one MCP source while the answer attributes it to another. Source-blind scoring sees support in the pooled evidence and passes it; ProvenanceGuard separately checks whether the supporting source matches the one the answer states or implies. Source: paper Figure 1.

This is why faithfulness scores, useful as they are, are not enough for MCP agents. An answer carries provenance, sometimes explicitly ("according to the account record") and sometimes implicitly. ProvenanceGuard keeps that connection between claim and source available for inspection.

ProvenanceGuard is a post-generation verification layer that sits on top of a black-box MCP agent. It runs after an agent produces an answer, and never collapses the evidence into one anonymous context. Instead it carries the source identity all the way through the pipeline. It reads the captured MCP trace, including the tool outputs and their source IDs, without retraining the agent. Then it does five things in sequence: it breaks the answer into specific claims, finds the source most relevant to each one, checks whether that source actually supports it, compares the source with the one the answer names or implies, and finally emits both a per-claim source verdict and a global, answer-level allow or block decision.

Sources indicate that the verification flow. Source identity is preserved through decomposition, routing, support scoring, attribution checking, and repair, rather than being pooled. Blocked answers can go through RARR-style repair and be re-verified. Source: paper Figure 2.

A few of the design choices are worth calling out. For the experiments in our paper, we used local models so the captured traces could be processed in a controlled, offline setup: MiniLM helps find the relevant source, a DeBERTa NLI verifier model checks whether that source supports the claim, and a local language model helps break answers into claims. The verifier also checks literal values closely: a number, date, or identifier absent from the source cannot pass merely because the sentence sounds plausible. A calibrated decision step combines these signals. If an answer is blocked, a RARR-style repair step can try a source-grounded revision or a safe fallback, which the verifier then checks again.

In a recent development, those named models are the setup we evaluated, not a requirement of ProvenanceGuard. The same claim, source, and decision steps can be adapted to hosted models where a team prefers cloud services; a new setup would need its own testing and calibration. Our reported results come from the local configuration. Its conservative decision policy suits data-sensitive review, where getting the source right matters more than producing the fastest possible answer.

It has been revealed that we tested ProvenanceGuard on answers from a medical agent that had used patient records, research articles, and other tools. This gave us 281 real traces to study. Medicine is a useful test because a fact from a patient's record and a fact from general research cannot be treated as the same source. The method can also be used in other fields when an agent keeps a record of its tool outputs and source IDs. For the main test, human experts checked 361 claims from 40 answers set aside from the data used to develop the system.

The most direct result is this: experts noted 139 claims should not pass, and ProvenanceGuard caught 138 of them. It let one through. It also held 67 claims that the experts considered supported, sending them for review or repair. This reflects the cautious setting we tested: it favors a second look at some supported claims over letting unsupported ones through. For claims with an identifiable source, it also picked the right source about 86% of the time in this test.

We ran four other support checkers on the same claims. ProvenanceGuard scored highest on the paper's measure of how well a system catches claims that should be blocked while avoiding unnecessary blocks. The other checkers in this comparison did not tell us which tool output supported each claim. ProvenanceGuard records that connection, so a reviewer can see the source checked for each claim and the decision it produced.

Sources indicate that binary support metrics on the same held-out claim packet. ProvenanceGuard matches or beats the source-blind baselines on blocking while also producing per-claim source verdicts. Source: paper abstract and Table III.

In a separate, harder test with several similar sources, ProvenanceGuard scored 0.846 F1 for deciding which claims to block, but identified the exact source correctly in 50.3% of claims. Telling similar sources apart remains an important area for improvement.

We also ran a controlled test focused on wrong attribution: we changed the named source in 50 cases while leaving the supporting evidence intact. ProvenanceGuard caught all 50 swaps. This shows it can detect a clear source error, while the harder test shows the challenge of choosing among many plausible sources.

Blocking is only useful if there is something to do with a blocked answer. Wired to the RARR-style repair loop, the full-trace run resolved all 173 blocked answers, though 144 of them ended in fallback text rather than a substantive rewrite, which is the system choosing to avoid an unverifiable answer rather than manufacture one. On reconstructed multi-source test traces, a fresh repair run resolved all 59 initially blocked answers with only two terminal fallbacks. As an offline gate the overhead is modest, roughly half a second per answer on the reported local configuration, with the NLI and routing calls themselves in the tens of milliseconds.

Recent findings suggest that as agents move from single-passage RAG to multi-tool MCP setups, the question of which source a fact actually came from stops being a footnote and becomes part of what factuality means. ProvenanceGuard makes that source connection visible claim by claim. For Multiverse Computing, that means a way to check existing agents while keeping sensitive traces in a controlled environment when needed. The medical study is one use case; the same approach can be adapted wherever an agent's trace preserves its tools and sources.

That adaptation is already visible in NVIDIA NVFlow, which merged an optional grounding-verification stage for its finance agent. It checks completed answers against the SEC excerpts the agent retrieved and saves separate decisions without changing the original rollout or training data. The NVFlow contribution uses ProvenanceGuard's source-aware verification approach; the repair loop discussed above belongs to the broader research system.

ProvenanceGuard was also presented as a poster at the Agentic AI Summit 2026 at UC Berkeley.

According to recent reports, want the full technical details, including the routing and NLI derivations, the calibration ablations, the multi-source stress slices, and the complete results tables? Read the full paper on Hugging Face, or get in touch with our team to talk about applying source-aware verification to your own agents.

The failure mode that matters for MCP agents is quieter than "hallucination": a claim that is true somewhere in the pooled tool outputs, attributed to the wrong source.

Source-blind faithfulness can still go green in that case — the fact exists in the soup. Source-aware verification is the contract upgrade: keep tool/source IDs through claim decomposition, support check, and attribution check, then allow/block with a per-claim source verdict a reviewer can actually inspect.

Recent findings suggest that practical ask for teams wiring MCP: when your eval notes "grounded," does it mean supported-by-any-tool-output, or supported-by-the-source-the-answer-named? Those are different release gates. In multi-tool setups the second one is the one that catches cross-source conflation before a human trusts the citation.

In a recent development, hi, thank you for your comment. You’ve captured the concern well. For ProvenanceGuard, when a claim is “grounded” it means it is supported by the source the answer names or implies. Finding the fact somewhere else in the tool outputs isn’t enough. In the refund-window example, the policy supports the fact, but the answer credits the account record, so we flag the mismatch and show the source verdict.

I had a brief read on the paper, but I could not find any comparison with cheaper llm agent for source aware judge. Like this is my reading of the paper;.

Sources indicate that like, it seems (2 - 5) can be done via basic prompts in lifecycle, if you own the executing agent. If not, this can also be done via hooks in harness as plugin. Do you have any comparison on this. Basically, how much of random forest, and all of these eng/plumbing is buying, vs second llm call over traces+ans?

Hi, fair question. A source-aware LLM judge could do these checks, and we don’t report a direct comparison with a cheaper one in the paper.

In a recent development, however, part of our motivation is that introducing an LLM judge can itself give inconsistent verdicts or confuse sources (the same kinds of errors we’re trying to catch). A second LLM call can therefore introduce fresh errors of its own. ProvenanceGuard uses explicit source tracking and calibrated support checks to reduce reliance on another generative judgment. The comparison you suggest would indeed be a useful further study to quantify the benefit in accuracy, latency and cost.

AWS Device Farm, a service for testing mobile and web apps, now provides Test Insights for Appium, Espresso, and XCUITest runs across multiple devices. Test Insights helps you and AI agents understand the health of your tests and resolve failures faster by providing a detailed breakdown of your test suite by device and by test.

With Test Insights, Device Farm's existing APIs now return enhanced test metadata, failure root cause with stack trace, a video for each test, start and stop times, median and average times spent on each device and test, and test counts by result. With this data in one place, your agents spend less time and fewer tokens looking for the root cause of test failures, and the AWS Device Farm troubleshooting skill uses it to help diagnose failed runs and suggest fixes. Test Insights is available alongside any default and custom test reports you generate, at no additional cost.

Test Insights is included in all AWS Regions where Device Farm is available.

💡 Key Takeaways

Recent findings suggest that amazon Route 53 now offers Advanced Hosted Zones, a newly introduced hosted zone tier with additional guardrails, visibility, and resilience features. Advanced Hosted Zones include Change Guardrails that prevent accidental record deletions, record-level Change History, and public DNS fallback in private hosted zones.

A single mistaken DNS change can take part of your domain offline, such as deleting a record that is still serving traffic or removing a delegation that resolvers are still using. To protect against this, customers build their own validation pipelines, review processes, and audit tooling. With Change Guardrails turned on, Route 53 checks each change before applying it. It blocks deleting a record that is still receiving DNS queries, a record that an alias record in the same hosted zone points to, or a delegation that is still in use. When a guardrail blocks a change, Route 53 rejects the whole request with an error that explains why, and no records change. Guardrails apply to every change, including changes from infrastructure as code tools. Change History gives you a record-level history of changes to your hosted zone, retained for 365 days, so you can see what changed and when.

In a recent development, to get started, create a new Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing hosted zone, then turn on the guardrails you want. You can use the Route 53 console, API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation. Advanced Hosted Zones are priced separately from Standard Hosted Zones. For rates, see the Route 53 pricing page.

It has been revealed that advanced Hosted Zones are available in all AWS commercial Regions where Route 53 public and private hosted zones are available. To learn more, see Advanced Hosted Zones in the Route 53 Developer Guide.

Advancing chip design with OpenAI models

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that openAI’s models are quickly improving the chips that power AI.
  • According to recent reports, to measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings.
  • Industry observers note that we started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that openAI’s models are quickly improving the chips that power AI. In August,⁠ we shared how OpenAI engineers used our frontier models to accelerate the development of our first custom inference chip, Jalapeño. Here, we look more closely at the expert-level design improvements behind the Jalapeño gains and how we’re applying the same approach to deliver significant gains on third-party hardware with AMD.

According to recent reports, to measure our model’s ability at end to end chip design tasks, we evaluated successive generations on two open-source processor designs with interesting findings. And to ground capability development in trusted evaluators, we’re working with Synopsys to integrate frontier intelligence with the electronic design automation (EDA) tools that engineers already use to design and verify chips.

Industry observers note that we started using GPT‑o3 mini to help design Jalapeño in early 2025. Even that early model found ways to make nontrivial PPA improvements, such as:.

In a recent development, in the vector unit, which manages and executes parallel computing tasks, the savings came from floating-point adders and multipliers, conversion functions, reduction logic, and the special-function unit. The models explored both alternative logic implementations and how to divide computations across pipeline stages, finding opportunities to share hardware and reduce intermediate storage.

In the matrix unit, an arithmetic component, improvements accumulated across floating-point adders, multipliers, and low-precision dot-product circuits. One multiplier redesign used about 15% less cell area in synthesis while reducing latency from two clock cycles to one. A separate adder redesign reduced cell area by about 15% while retaining its two-cycle latency. Further improvements to dot-product logic and pipeline organization contributed additional savings across the block.

Sources indicate that across the broader Jalapeño design effort, the team estimates that model proposed changes reduced standard-cell area by about 13% in the vector unit and 10% in the matrix unit. These optimizations were silicon proven during Jalapeño’s silicon bring-up⁠.

We have partnered with AMD on PPA improvements and seen up to 14% improvement relative to heavily optimized baselines on the flagship GPU IP. Our model identified further improvements by rewriting the code that describes the chip’s circuits (SystemVerilog RTL). This represents roughly a year of progress achieved in less than 5 months–unprecedented results at the frontier of chip design. AMD has already included some of these changes in a recent design it sent for manufacturing, and added others to its production design files for use in future versions.

We’ve observed the model reason about RTL at the level of an expert microarchitect. The model can rewrite circuits that perform calculations, control operations, or move data. It used Synopsys tools to verify that each rewrite preserved the block’s behavior and to evaluate the trade-offs in power, performance, and area.

It has been revealed that AMD also verified single-digit percentage gains in PPA across key blocks of its upcoming next-generation flagship CPU using designs written by our model. Looking ahead, we expect further PPA improvements on top of GPU and CPU relative to the most optimized baseline.

Our results on Jalapeño and AMD’s chips show that models can make improvements in production designs. To measure the progression in chip design capabilities from one model generation to the next, we tested each model on two open-source 32-bit RISC-V cores. PicoRV32 is a compact core designed for reprogrammable chips called FPGAs. OpenTitan uses Ibex as the embedded processor in its security chip. Each is a complete processor core for embedded, microcontroller class workloads.

We gave each model the original hardware description for each core and asked it to increase throughput (the number of instructions the core can execute per second). For example, a change might let a core finish an instruction in fewer clock cycles but make each cycle take longer. Measuring throughput captures both effects.

We checked each design’s outputs in simulation. Designs scored zero if they failed a check or used more than 16 times the original core’s area. For designs that passed, we measured instructions per clock cycle on workloads hidden from the models. We took the geometric mean across those workloads and multiplied it by the maximum clock frequency estimated with Yosys. That gave us an estimate of instructions per second. For each core, we assigned the best throughput we observed under the same constraints a score of 1.0. The charts show the average score across runs, including those that scored zero.

It has been revealed that with a comparable budget of about 112,000 tokens per run, GPT‑6.2 Astra had the highest average score on both cores. GPT‑6.1 Sol also outscored GPT‑5.6 Sol on both.

Sources indicate that on the existing PicoRV32 core, GPT‑6.2 Astra has the highest mean score at the larger comparable budgets. Around 112,000 tokens, its score is about twice GPT‑6 Astra’s.

It has been revealed that on the existing Ibex core, GPT‑6.2 Astra’s mean score continues to climb across the higher budgets it reaches. GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol are closer together.

For the second task, we gave each model written requirements and templates from the open-source code showing how the core connects to the rest of the system. The model chose how data would move through the core and how to divide the work into stages. For each core, we kept the correctness checks, memory and cache settings, and throughput objectives the same as in the RTL optimization task.

Industry observers note that at about 112,000 tokens per run, all five models scored higher when they designed a core from written requirements than when they tried to improve the existing design. That held for both PicoRV32 and Ibex. GPT‑6.2 Astra gained more on Ibex than on PicoRV32. The full evaluation included 9,881 scored runs across both tasks, both cores, and all token budgets.

Starting from a PicoRV32 specification, GPT‑6.2 Astra passes a mean score of 0.7 near 112,000 tokens and scores higher at the next two observed budgets.

On Ibex, GPT‑6.2 Astra averages about 0.75 near 112,000 tokens when designing from a specification. Its curve stays above the others at larger shared budgets.

It has been revealed that starting from written requirements gives the models room to omit features found in the original cores, such as performance counters and additional instructions. Those features may do little to improve throughput on the test workloads, which could explain part of the score advantage. Requiring those features, setting a tighter limit on circuit area, and checking timing after physical synthesis would make the test more representative of production chip design.

Sources indicate that we have demonstrated that our models can explore upcoming processor architectures in RISC-V evals and contributed net new improvements on top of sophisticated production designs such as Jalapeño and AMD’s next generation flagship GPU and CPU. To ground model development in trusted evaluators and broaden the design challenges addressed, we’re partnering with Synopsys to train GPT‑Synopsys⁠(opens in a new window), a new model, to use Synopsys electronic design automation (EDA) tools the way expert chip designers do.

Industry News: Open TTS Leaderboard: Scalable Evaluation for Multilingual Text-to-Speech and Voice Cloning

📅 30 Sep 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1397 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible.
  • Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized.
  • These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that the pace of open-source text-to-speech (TTS) model releases has been incredible. On the Hugging Face Hub (as of Sep 30, 2026) there are more than 8K TTS models available 🚀.

Evaluation, however, hasn't kept pace: it remains fragmented and unstandardized. The gold standard is human preference scores such as MOS or MUSHRA (more on metrics). To this end, several arena-based leaderboards have established themselves as useful reference points for the community:.

These arenas compare models by presenting users with TTS outputs from two models, and asking them to choose one over the other. After collecting a sufficient number of votes, an Elo score is computed to rank models, typically with the Bradley–Terry model (see Voice Arena methodology).

It has been revealed that while human preference is the ultimate decider, arenas cannot scale to keep up with the pace of TTS releases. This may partly explain why open-source models are underrepresented on arena-style leaderboards: as of Sep 30, 2026, only 16 of the 92 models on Artificial Analysis are open-weights, with a similar skew on Voice Arena. This likely reflects practical factors: adding an API model requires little more than an API key, whereas an open model must be hosted and served by the arena operator, and commercial providers have more reason to seek placement than open-source authors. Another limitation with arena-style evaluation is voter consistency: no arena can ensure that the same voters with the same criteria of “better” can consistently evaluate models over time. Even the preferences of a single person change over time (“A man cannot step into the same river twice” as famously said by Heraclitus).

To this end, we've built the Open TTS Leaderboard, which uses objective metrics to evaluate models on complementary aspects of performance:.

By relying on objective metrics evaluating a model drops from a couple weeks (for collecting votes) to a couple hours ⚡.

Importantly, the Open TTS Leaderboard does not replace human preference ranking. ASR-based WER provides a proxy for intelligibility, while speaker similarity estimates voice identity preservation. Neither directly measures naturalness, expressiveness, or listener preference. Nevertheless, they can even inform voting-based leaderboards which models to include in their evaluations.

Our intention with this leaderboard is for it to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. The next few sections give an overview of main features of the Open TTS Leaderboard.

From the default view of the leaderboard, models are ranked by macro-average WER on the English splits of Seed TTS Eval (paper) and CV3 Eval (zero shot) (paper).

hexgrad/Kokoro-82M, Supertone/supertonic-3, and fishaudio/s2-pro lead the pack on English WER when averaged on these two splits, while the Pareto plots visualize which models strike a good balance between WER, batched inference (RTFx), and size.

English performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

k2-fsa/OmniVoice, fishaudio/s2-pro, and FunAudioLLM/Fun-CosyVoice3-0.5B-2512 are strong multilingual models.

By toggling “Voice cloning”, the models that support this functionality (on the selected languages) can be compared.

Moreover, a SIM column for speaker similarity now appears in the table, as well as two more Pareto plots for visualizing the tradeoff between SIM, batched inference, and size.

The average WER of some models, such as bosonai/higgs-tts-3-4b and openbmb/VoxCPM2, improve under voice cloning, namely when a reference audio is provided.

Recent findings suggest that numbers only tell part of the story, and as mentioned earlier human preference is the ultimate decider. From the “Listen” tab, you can compare the generated outputs that are behind the metrics, to find which model(s) you prefer!

Pick the language/dataset you're interested in, whether you want to compare voice cloning, and optionally pick the models or listen to outputs from a random selection.

The “Listen” tab fills an notable gap in existing TTS leaderboards: a space to explore model outputs of various models.

You can even give feedback on the generated outputs. As we collect more votes from the community, we may include this data on the leaderboard. So vote! But please login with your HF account to help us weed out spam/bots.

It has been revealed that the “Streaming” tab compares the streaming capabilities. Models are ranked by TTFA (time-to-first-audio), which quantifies how long a user waits after probing a model in order to obtain audio that can be played. This is vital for voice agents and other interactive apps.

It has been revealed that for streaming models (✅ under “Streaming API”) it's the time until the first audio chunk arrives. For non-streaming models, it's the time until the whole utterance is generated, because playback can't start any earlier. Every model runs one audio at a time (batch size 1), on the same 50 English prompts from CV3-Eval, on the same hardware and in its default voice. We drop the first 3 runs as warm-up and report the median TTFA across the rest.

It has been revealed that the default view compares performance on an H200 GPU. Results are also available for CPU for a small (but growing) set of models!

kyutai/pocket-tts is a great model for streaming on both GPU and CPU!

Recent findings suggest that the goal of the Open TTS Leaderboard is not only to keep up with the incredible pace of TTS model releases, but to be shaped by the community; we want to hear your feedback so the evaluations stay relevant and insightful. Let us know which datasets, models, and metrics you want to see!

We will soon open-source the evaluation scripts, much like the Open ASR Leaderboard repo, so that you can directly provide your feedback and suggestions via GitHub Concerns and PRs! Let's shape TTS evaluations together 🤗.

Glad this board splits multilingual TTS quality from voice-cloning identity instead of one aggregate green.

According to recent reports, the check I'd keep reading: whether the ranking still holds when you hold language/domain fixed versus when cloning is the axis. Otherwise teams optimize the easier subscale and still call the result "SOTA TTS.".

Recent findings suggest that english performance doesn't necessarily translate to other languages. Multiple languages can be toggled to rank models on multilingual performance. Seed TTS Eval only has movie box audio for English and Chinese, so the other languages are simply the score on CV3 Eval (zero shot). Note that Chinese, Japanese, and Korean are character-based languages and so character error rate (CER) is reported, and the “Average WER” across languages is a macro-average across languages.

Recent findings suggest that open TTS Leaderboard is an open evaluation platform designed to make multilingual text-to-speech and voice-cloning models easier to compare at scale. Traditional TTS arenas usually let customers listen to outputs from two models and choose the one they prefer. Those votes can then be used to calculate an Elo-style score, often through approaches such as the Bradley–Terry model, giving users a simple way to understand how different systems perform based on human preference.

Human feedback remains an important part of evaluating speech quality, but relying only on arena-style voting can be difficult as new TTS models are released at a rapid pace. Open-source models can also face practical barriers because they generally need to be hosted and served by the evaluation platform, while API-based commercial models can be added more easily. This can result in open-weight systems being less visible on public leaderboards. Another challenge is consistency: people's preferences and listening criteria can change over time, meaning that votes collected months apart may not always represent exactly the same standards.

Open TTS Leaderboard aims to address these challenges by providing a scalable and transparent space for evaluating multilingual TTS and voice-cloning systems. The goal is to make comparisons easier to reproduce, expand coverage of open models, and provide useful evaluation signals alongside human preference. By bringing together scalable testing and community feedback, the project can help researchers, developers, and users better understand how speech models perform across different languages, voices, and use cases.

Recent findings suggest that gitHub repo with the eval scripts is public! https://github.com/huggingface/open-tts-leaderboard.

The Blueprint: How Kult built a gaming companion that actually knows your game

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1330 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies.
  • Industry observers note that kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games.
  • Sources indicate that traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

In a recent development, welcome to The Blueprint, our ongoing series where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

Industry observers note that kult is a London-based startup building a companion experience for games. It sits alongside your session, understands the game you are playing and where you are in it, and answers by voice and on a second screen. The more you play with it, the better it knows how you like to play.

Sources indicate that traditionally, getting help in the middle of a game meant alt-tabbing, opening a video, scrolling a forum, and hoping you find the answer before you forget why you looked. Information should come to the player instead. As gamers ourselves, our team wanted a way for someone to be able to ask a question out loud, hands on the keyboard or controller, hear an answer, and consult a second screen if needed, without interrupting their immersion in the game.

Three things decide whether that works: latency, accuracy and cost.

Recent findings suggest that latency: Games are time-sensitive. The answer has to be fast, and the interaction should feel like asking a friend who’s an expert on the game, sitting on the couch next to you and watching you play.

Accuracy: General-purpose models have training cutoffs. They can be months out of date and are often wrong about a specific game, patch, or build — and a wrong answer can be costly in the game and a waste of the player's time. Every game also has its own items, systems, and vocabulary, so accuracy has to hold across hundreds of games. The right answer also depends on the player: The same question deserves a different answer 10 minutes into a game than a 100 hours in.

Cost: An always-on companion handles many turns per session, so every turn has to be inexpensive enough for a consumer product. Covering hundreds of games is only possible if adding one is cheap and takes no manual work.

Recent findings suggest that given these needs, we knew we would want a range of models to build Kult. Fortunately, Google’s Gemini models have some of the greatest variety in terms of balancing performance and especially cost, and with the Model Garden in Gemini platform, we have access to hundreds of models beyond Gemini. Gemini models have became the default family on both sides of the system: the live conversation, and the knowledge behind it, dynamically match the right model for every task.

Recent findings suggest that the lightest Gemini Flash tier handles high-volume, repetitive work, where we make thousands of small calls for every game we add. Gemini Flash runs every conversational turn. It works out what the player is asking and writes an answer grounded in our knowledge of that game, fast enough to keep up with play. The latest and most advanced Gemini models handle the rare, heavy reasoning we do once per game.

Industry observers note that having that range on one API surface matters to a small team. The latest Gemini Flash models in particular sit at a point of price, speed, and quality that we have not found elsewhere, and they are the reason an always-on gaming companion works as a consumer product.

In a recent development, we reach the models through both the Gemini platform and the Gemini Developer API, with a routing layer that picks the backend for each model. Our backend runs on Google Kubernetes Engine.

It has been revealed that every answer comes in two parts. The voice gives the short version. At the same moment, a visual answer lands in a feed on the player's second screen: images, embedded video, maps, builds, interactive tools made for that game, and links to the guides and creators behind the answer.

We build that feed with Google's open standard for agent-generated interfaces. The model does not write code. It describes the interface it wants using a catalog of components we designed, and the app renders it natively in Kult's own style. That keeps the feed safe and consistent, and lets us add new kinds of visual answers, and new devices, without rebuilding the front end.

According to recent reports, kult now covers more than 100 games, and adding a game is an automated process, not a manual project. That’s a key part of what lets a small team aim at any game a player picks up, including new releases, where most of the playing happens in the first weeks.

We are in alpha with our first players and opening up to more over the coming months. As we have grown, we have built a close working relationship with the Google Cloud team, with direct access to their engineers when we need it. That matters when every model generation raises the ceiling of what a gaming companion product can do.

This expertise, both within the models and our supportive partners, allows us to focus on our passion: building the features gamers want, faster and better than any possible competition.

Five principles shape how Kult works.

Answers come from knowledge we build, not from what a model happens to remember. A game can change with every patch. For each game we cover, Kult builds a structured knowledge base automatically and keeps it current, and the model's job is to reason over that knowledge.

In a recent development, the answer depends on who is asking. Kult keeps track of your session: the game, what you have been doing, and what you asked a moment ago. "What is he weak to?" needs no further explanation, because Kult already knows which boss you’re facing. Over time it learns from how you play, what you ask about and what you ignore, and shapes its answers around you. A player who wants the fastest route and one who wants to find everything should not get the same replies.

Recent findings suggest that the player is never left in silence. Kult responds straight away and carries the conversation while the deeper reasoning runs behind it. The spoken answer is short, and the visual feed carries everything the voice cannot.

Industry observers note that the smallest model that can do the job does the job. Much of the work in a system like ours is a decision, not a piece of writing. It needs to understand which game the query is about, does the question need a lookup, did the answer cover the point.

Sources indicate that for decisions like these we use Jev, a decision-only model that returns a choice with a calibrated confidence score. Confident cases are settled in a fraction of a second at a fraction of the cost, and uncertain ones escalate to a larger Gemini model. Every model sits behind a registry, so when a upcoming generation ships, we benchmark it against reference answers written by people who know the games, and swap it in if it wins.

Recent findings suggest that every question makes Kult better. Taken together, the questions players ask about a game show us where its knowledge is thin and what to build next. We are designing Kult so that this loop tightens with every session. The more people play, the richer the knowledge becomes for everyone. Every session teaches a player something, as well as the entire Kult system, and Kult helps them keep it. We think the companion that sits beside the game is only the start.

Next is computer vision. In the coming months, Kult will start to see what is happening in your game, so the companion can be aware of the moment without being asked. We’re using Google's Live models as part of that work, for video understanding and more.

If you are a gamer, try it for yourself www.joinkult.gg.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports customer managed keys (CMK) in AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for data encryption at rest.
  • In a recent development, lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code.
  • In a recent development, to get started, create a CMK in AWS KMS and configure its cryptographic properties, metadata, and AWS IAM access permissions.

Sources indicate that AWS Lambda MicroVMs now supports customer managed keys (CMK) in AWS Key Management Service (KMS) for data encryption at rest. CMK gives you full control over the lifecycle and usage of your KMS keys, helping meet compliance requirements in regulated industries like financial services and healthcare.

In a recent development, lambda MicroVMs is a serverless compute primitive that provides VM-level isolation, near-instant launch and resume, and state preservation for executing user or AI generated code. Use MicroVMs to build applications like AI coding assistants, interactive development environments, and vulnerability scanners.

In a recent development, to get started, create a CMK in AWS KMS and configure its cryptographic properties, metadata, and AWS IAM access permissions. Then, specify this CMK as a parameter when you create a MicroVM image or run a MicroVM. Lambda uses this CMK to encrypt your MicroVM image, MicroVM image environment variables, and the payload passed to the MicroVM run hook. You can use CMK with Lambda MicroVMs through the AWS Lambda console, AWS CloudFormation, AWS Cloud Development Kit, or with your preferred Agentic development tools using the Agent Toolkit for AWS.

​​CMK support for MicroVMs is available in the following AWS Regions: Asia Pacific (Hong Kong), Asia Pacific (Malaysia), Asia Pacific (Mumbai), Asia Pacific (Seoul), Asia Pacific (Singapore), Asia Pacific (Sydney), Asia Pacific (Thailand), Asia Pacific (Tokyo), Europe (Frankfurt), Europe (Ireland), Europe (Spain), Europe (Stockholm), South America (São Paulo), US East (N. Virginia), US East (Ohio), and US West (Oregon). To learn more about Lambda MicroVMs, visit the AWS Lambda MicroVMs developer guide. For information on pricing for CMK, see AWS KMS pricing.​.

#20421. Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment

AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Managing frontier AI risk: From training to deployment

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2440 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that the capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead.
  • It has been revealed that since the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models.
  • We use defense in depth with multiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that the capabilities of frontier models are rapidly accelerating, and our ability to understand, align, and secure them must stay ahead. We are pacing the development and release of our models, including pausing internal training⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) or holding back models like GPT‑6.1 Astra when we need more time to meet our safety standards. We’ve introduced new processes such as safety cases and require stronger evidence of aligned behavior throughout training. These requirements slow the pace of model releases, but they give us greater confidence to safely move forward.

It has been revealed that since the Hugging Face incident⁠ in July, we've strengthened safeguards and alignment requirements for how we train, test, and deploy models. This post explains how we evaluate and manage risk at each stage, from highly sandboxed training environments to the Codex deployment you use on your computer. We evaluate both models and safeguards at each stage, requiring a safety review to advance to the next stage.

We use defense in depth with multiple layers of protection that reduce dependence on any single safeguard. If one layer fails, others help prevent harm, limit consequences, or alert us so we can intervene.

We organize our protections around four layers:.

Industry observers note that effective monitoring depends on model monitorability - how reliably monitors can detect mistakes or unsafe behavior from a model’s reasoning and actions. For example, a model that verbalizes its intention to cheat in its chain-of-thought (CoT) is more monitorable than one that omits this information. We evaluate monitorability during training and before deployment, develop better methods for measuring⁠(opens in a new window) it, and study what affects it⁠(opens in a new window).

In a recent development, the Hugging Face incident highlighted why we should not rely on sandboxing alone to contain highly capable models. We now monitor frontier models across most internal and external deployment settings, including all internal deployments that use tools.

The role of each layer changes across three stages of model development and deployment:.

Research: We train, test, and use models in sandboxed environments.

Internal deployment: OpenAI employees use models for practical work.

External deployment: Models become available to people and organizations more broadly.

It has been revealed that we rely on different layers at different stages. During training, when alignment is less certain, we depend more heavily on sandboxing and monitoring. As models gain broader access during deployment, alignment and system-level controls become increasingly important. At each stage, we evaluate whether the combined protections are sufficient for the model’s capabilities and access. Our determinations may be reviewed with our Safety Advisory Group (SAG) and overseen by the Safety and Security Committee (SSC) of the OpenAI Foundation’s Board of Directors.

During the research phase, we evaluate models to gain confidence in their alignment properties. Because we cannot yet fully rely on alignment to prevent harm, we rely heavily on security and sandboxing to restrict what they can access and do.

Industry observers note that based on the current state of alignment research, monitoring systems, and the security of internet infrastructure, we believe the responsible approach is to conduct frontier model training with no live internet access. After the Hugging Face incident, we significantly restructured our internal research systems to contain models using:.

sandboxes that restrict the privileges of the model.

virtual machines to further isolate the workload from the underlying computer.

network and cloud perimeters that cut the entire cluster off from the internet.

Sources indicate that we continuously red-team this system, having teams of our strongest models try to reach the live internet, escape security boundaries, or communicate with agents they are meant to be isolated from. This helps us test whether containment holds against the capabilities of the models it is intended to constrain.

According to recent reports, as an additional layer of defense, we monitor all frontier inference to detect if the model has bypassed our security invariants. If our monitoring detects that the model has reached the internet, we page our security teams and autopause the workload.

Monitoring provides a critical backstop when containment fails. In a recent misalignment report, we shared that monitors detected an internal research model exploiting a DNS misconfiguration⁠(opens in a new window) to gain limited internet access. We paused training and evaluation of our most capable models from September 20th to October 1st while we investigated and addressed the security gap.

Industry observers note that to make interventions fast and reliable, we built Control Room⁠, a central system that tracks research workloads and stops further model output within 35 seconds of receiving an instruction to halt a job. These controls are enforced directly in the inference infrastructure, so they do not depend on each research workload implementing its own shutdown mechanism. For frontier-model research workloads, they also stop model output if Control Room becomes unavailable.

Sources indicate that red-teaming and monitoring work together. We cannot guarantee that a sandbox is impenetrable, but red-teaming helps us assess how much effort a model would need to escape it. The more effort the model requires, the more the opportunity for monitors to detect and stop it.

We mandate strong security and monitoring controls at the research stage for a few reasons:.

In a recent development, models are still being evaluated. Some have not yet completed the safety training, alignment audits, and reviews required for public release.

Industry observers note that frontier research settings can amplify risks. Certain research tasks require more ambitious setups, making the model more persistent or capable than typically seen during external deployment (for example, a team of 10,000 agents was required to solve the Navier Stokes problem).

Training runs at scale with less direct human oversight. Unlike a typical Codex session, our training workloads involve large numbers of model actions without a person following each interaction.

In a recent development, before broad release, employees switch from sandboxed research use of frontier models to unsandboxed internal use, e.g. making the model accessible in ChatGPT to employees. This gives us a better understanding of how the models behave in practical settings⁠(opens in a fresh window), and informs deployment decisions.

During this phase, we give the model access to the broader internet, our Slack, our codebase, and internal infrastructure. This is a significant change in risk, as the model’s actions now have a direct impact on the systems we use to build and run OpenAI. During internal deployment, we need to rely more on model alignment, system safeguards, and monitoring as opposed to security controls.

According to recent reports, before a frontier model can be deployed outside of the sandbox, it must first go through alignment and monitorability testing⁠(opens in a new window). We have a suite of alignment evaluations, which test both for specific alignment failure modes (such as circumventing safety and security restrictions) and broad measurements of propensity (such as resampling internal Codex trajectories and checking for misalignment). You can see more about our alignment and monitorability evaluations in the latest GPT‑6 Astra system card⁠(opens in a new window).

Sources indicate that mimicking our production setups, we add an additional layer of defense with system-level classifiers, which are designed to protect against frontier harms such as cyberabuse and bioweaponization. We also generally require Auto-Review⁠(opens in a new window) for employees using Codex, which evaluates potentially risk actions and escalates them back to the user.

Finally, we monitor for misaligned behavior on every frontier inference during internal deployment. Since the model now has expanded privileges and access to internal information and systems, risks such as data exfiltration, or sending sensitive data to an unauthorized destination, become especially important to detect. Monitoring also helps us investigate new forms of misalignment⁠(opens in a new window).

Public deployment exposes models to far more users, tasks, and environments, increasing both the scale and variety of risks. At this stage, we also need to protect against potentially malicious actors who purposefully direct the model to perform harm.

According to recent reports, before public release, models and system safeguards must meet our external deployment safety requirements. We assess them through:.

According to recent reports, performing a larger suite of alignment and safety evaluations. For our frontier models, this includes performing new rounds of adaptive testing⁠ with our internal automated redteamers to stress-test the robustness of the model. We publish the results of our capability and safety evaluations in our system cards⁠(opens in a new window).

For our most capable models, we also perform testing with third parties to stress-test both our safeguards against misuse and the underlying alignment of our models.

Examining monitoring flags from the internal deployment stage to track any changes in the base model’s underlying alignment.

Industry observers note that in addition to our “synchronous” safeguards (such as model safety training and system classifiers), for external deployments we also leverage offline enforcement and investigation. These teams use a combination of scaled agentic investigators and human review to detect and identify potential threat actors, ranging from cyberabuse, bioweaponization, distillation⁠, and misalignment from the model itself. Offline enforcement is especially helpful to gather information across accounts in order to build a more holistic picture of a potential threat.

Trusted access programs, such as Daybreak and Rosalind⁠, offer another layer of security, and accelerate defenders and legitimate researchers while restricting access by potential attackers.

When we notice a failure in one of our layers of safety, regardless of whether any harm actually occurred, we want to quickly investigate, triage, and if possible and appropriate, disclose the failure externally. Under our misalignment reporting⁠ policy, any employee can flag an incident for public disclosure. These reports are investigated, and if there is a disagreement on whether they should be externally disclosed, the decision is escalated to our Safety Advisory Group (SAG). In addition to relying on employee reports, we proactively look for misalignment incidents so we can address them and share findings.

You can see our misalignment reports here⁠(opens in a latest window).

Recent findings suggest that this work depends on both research progress and operational discipline: configuring controls correctly, testing how they interact, and responding decisively when they fail. A misconfigured network service or a failed automatic stop can undermine otherwise strong protections.

As models gain newly introduced capabilities, we will need to keep challenging the assumptions behind our safeguards and improving them where necessary. Lessons from research, internal use, and public deployment must inform how we train, evaluate, and deploy the next models.

We will continue sharing findings through system cards, incident reports, internal deployment risk reports⁠(opens in a new window), and external evaluations⁠ so that others can scrutinize our approach, including its limitations. When that evidence falls short of the bar we hold for safety, we will again pause training or withhold release until those requirements are met.

Pacing model development in an era of cyber-critical capabilities — How we slowed frontier training while strengthening containment, expanding monitoring, and requiring stronger evidence of alignment.

Towards safety cases for frontier AI training — Initial guidelines for evidence-based safety arguments covering technical safeguards, operational practices, and investigations of misalignment.

Priorities and principles for effective third party assessments⁠ — Our proposed approach to independent scrutiny of safety cases, safeguards, evaluations, and model behavior.

Periodic Summary of Internal Use Catastrophic-Risk Assessments⁠(opens in a new window) — Our public report covering June–September 2026 describes internal frontier-model deployments, their assessed risks, and changes to safeguards and governance.

Defining and evaluating aligned behavior.

An updated Model Spec for more capable and beneficial AI⁠ — How we updated the Model Spec around five core values to guide models’ judgment, behavior, and respect for human oversight.

Eval-production behavior gaps in agent safety and the role of eval-awareness⁠(opens in a upcoming window) — A study of differences between safety-evaluation results and production behavior, including how models’ interpretations of evaluation objectives affect performance.

Beyond g-mean²: complementary metrics for monitorability⁠(opens in a upcoming window) — New metrics for comparing monitorability and estimating residual risk in simulated systems where monitors reject model outputs.

GPT‑6 Astra System Card⁠(opens in a upcoming window) — Detailed evaluations of Astra’s capabilities, safety, alignment, and monitorability, alongside its deployment safeguards and limitations.

Containing models and improving safeguards.

Securing our frontier model training environment — How we strengthened isolation, built offline research environments, and used our strongest models to test containment boundaries.

Training activation classifiers for safety and alignment⁠(opens in a upcoming window) — How classifiers use models’ internal activations to detect potentially harmful behavior and interrupt responses or tool calls.

Auto-review of agent actions without synchronous human oversight⁠(opens in a new window) — How a separate review agent assesses actions that cross sandbox boundaries, helping coding agents work autonomously while blocking potentially harmful or unauthorized actions.

GPT‑Red: Unlocking Self-Improvement for Robustness⁠ — How we train automated red-teamers through self-play to discover vulnerabilities and improve models’ robustness against prompt injections.

Control Room⁠ — How we track workloads across our research infrastructure and enforce rapid stops to model output when safety or security concerns require intervention.

Incident response and disclosure.

How we detect frontier model misalignment — Our monitoring system combines activation probes, model-based review, automated investigation, and human response to detect and investigate concerning behavior.

The Hugging Face incident and the road ahead⁠ — Our findings from the Hugging Face incident and the changes it prompted across security, monitoring, and alignment.

An agent used DNS to reach an external chatbot⁠(opens in a upcoming window) — How a research model bypassed internet restrictions through insufficient DNS filtering, how monitoring detected it, and the controls added afterward.

Disrupting a coordinated model-distillation campaign⁠ — How we investigated and disrupted attempts to extract protected model reasoning through account enforcement, technical controls, and partner coordination.

Our framework for reporting model misalignment⁠ — Our process for tracking, investigating, and disclosing concerning model behavior, including cases whose causes or significance remain uncertain.

Misalignment Reports and Notices⁠(opens in a upcoming window) — Our collection of disclosed incidents and notices showing how misalignment arises and where safeguards succeed or fail.

Research progress and applications.

Research acceleration: The view inside OpenAI — Early evidence of how coding agents are changing research inside OpenAI, including their growing use, increasingly complex tasks, and effects on experimentation.

On the Navier–Stokes Millennium Prize Problem — A mathematical proof produced by an internal AI system, accompanied by a Lean formalization, illustrating the capabilities of large-scale research deployments.

Daybreak — Our cybersecurity program provides vetted defenders with advanced AI capabilities, security tools, and support to find vulnerabilities and strengthen defenses.

Introducing GPT‑Rosalind for life sciences research⁠ — A specialized model for biology, drug discovery, and translational medicine, available to eligible organizations through a trusted-access program.

Industry News: AutoSynthData: Generating Training Data for Enterprise Agents

📅 02 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments.
  • In a recent development, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data.
  • At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that enterprises need agents that work well in their own environments. The work they ask these agents to do is shaped by the systems they use, the rules they follow, and the state of their data. A model may be broadly capable and still struggle with a particular environment: a workflow it handles poorly, a combination of tools it misuses, or a constraint it fails to respect. Those are the weaknesses an enterprise needs to improve.

In a recent development, the difficulty is turning those weaknesses into training data. An individual failure tells us something, but training a model requires many fresh tasks that exercise the same capability in different situations. Those tasks must also be possible to complete in the environment, resemble work someone would actually request, and have a reliable way to check whether the agent succeeded.

At ServiceNow CoreAI, we built AutoSynthData to turn those capability gaps into training data. It uses a target model’s failures and a stronger teacher’s successes to decide what the model should learn next, then generates and validates latest tasks that exercise those capabilities. As the model improves, the curriculum shifts toward what it still finds difficult. We illustrate the pipeline with EnterpriseOps Gym (Malay et al., 2026), using the released dataset. We begin by describing the environment an agent operates in and what makes a task useful for training.

An agentic environment defines the world in which an agent operates: the state it can observe and modify, the tools and APIs it can invoke, and the state transitions produced by its actions.

A task is instantiated within this environment. We use the following abstraction:.

The system specification defines the constraints under which the agent operates, including system instructions, environment policies, and, when applicable, task-specific initialization such as a seeded database state or a set of knowledge articles.

Industry observers note that the specification must be compatible with the environment’s tools, state, and supported actions. Its instructions should be clear and avoid arbitrary constraints introduced solely to manufacture difficulty.

The user prompt specifies what the user wants the agent to accomplish, together with any user-level constraints. A generated task should satisfy three properties.

In a recent development, feasibility. There should exist at least one trajectory in the current environment that satisfies the user prompt while respecting the system specification. This rules out tasks that depend on unavailable tools, inaccessible knowledge, impossible state transitions, or actions prohibited by policy.

Realism. The user prompt should resemble something a user would plausibly ask in the target environment. The space of executable behaviors is usually much larger than the space of realistic workflows.

Difficulty. For training, the task should expose a weakness of the current agent. Tasks that are already solved reliably provide little fresh training signal. The useful region is therefore tasks that are feasible and realistic, but not yet consistently solved.

Industry observers note that the verifier determines whether the resulting trajectory successfully completes the task. It should satisfy three properties.

Consistency. It should agree with the user prompt, the system specification, and the task-specific environment state.

Soundness. It should reject trajectories that fail to satisfy the task or violate relevant constraints.

In a recent development, completeness. It should accept valid solutions rather than encode one particular reference trajectory.

These properties matter directly during training. A lax verifier can reward incorrect behavior, while an overly restrictive verifier can penalize valid solutions.

Sources indicate that given an environment and a target model, AutoSynthData generates training tasks consisting of a system specification, user prompt, and verifier. The generated tasks are grounded in the environment and selected to provide useful training signal for the current model.

Sources indicate that autoSynthData first evaluates the target model in the environment using diagnostic tasks and identifies patterns in the tasks it struggles to complete. A stronger teacher helps characterize which of those tasks are solvable and what successful behavior looks like. AutoSynthData turns the resulting capability gaps into upcoming executable tasks, checks each task in the environment, and uses accepted samples for post-training. Evaluating the updated model reveals which gaps remain and can guide the next round of generation.

Industry observers note that autoSynthData uses evaluation runs in the target environment to identify what the model needs to learn next. In our EnterpriseOps Gym experiment, we run both the target model and a stronger teacher on the evaluation tasks. We examine those runs to identify:.

We distill these findings into sanitized capability specification cards. The evaluation tasks guide what the model should learn, but the generator does not receive their original prompts, entities, trajectories, or verifier details. It receives the cards and uses them to create new tasks with different prompts, states, and solution paths.

Identifying a capability gap tells us what to teach, but training requires many varied tasks that exercise it. AutoSynthData uses the specification card to generate those tasks.

Suppose the target model struggles with tasks that require the following workflow:.

Industry observers note that the generator creates new tasks that exercise this workflow, varying the entities, initial environment state, workflow composition, tool combinations, wording, and difficulty. The stronger teacher then demonstrates a successful trajectory for each task. For supervised fine-tuning (SFT), these demonstrations teach the target model how to apply the capability in new situations.

AutoSynthData builds the dataset in two phases: first generating and validating core samples, then expanding them into novel variants.

Industry observers note that the target phase creates the core set of training samples from the capability specifications. Workers generate independent tasks in parallel, picking up a fresh target when they finish. Each candidate goes through validation, execution, solver evaluation, and repair before acceptance. The result is a batch of vetted examples built around what the target model needs to learn.

The multiply phase expands the dataset by creating novel variants of accepted target samples. Each variant has its own user request, environment state, entity configuration, reference trajectory, and verifier, and must pass the same validation and execution checks. A multiplied sample cannot seed another multiplied sample. This anchors expansion to the vetted target set and limits drift across generations.

It has been revealed that to support both phases, AutoSynthData separates generation control from environment-specific execution. A shared controller coordinates generation, quality control, coverage, and dataset construction, while an adapter handles environment execution, task and state management, reference replay, deterministic verification, solver execution, and task profiling.

Sources indicate that together, parallel target generation and multiplication provide a path to training-scale datasets. Their usefulness depends on the checks applied to every candidate: the task must be executable, the solution must work, and the verifier must distinguish success from failure.

In a recent development, generating a plausible request is not enough to produce useful training data. A task may be impossible in the target environment, its reference solution may fail when executed, or its verifier may reward the wrong final state. AutoSynthData checks these properties before accepting a task for training.

AutoSynthData reviews quality at two levels: individual candidates must pass verification, and batches must provide useful coverage and diversity.

Each candidate must clear a quality-control loop before entering the training dataset. We begin with solver evaluation to measure difficulty. In the configuration used here, we favor tasks the target model solves on no more than one of three trials and the stronger solver solves on at least two of three trials. Candidates also undergo positive and negative verification and a bounded repair process.

The positive gate asks: Does the intended solution solve the generated task?

In a recent development, the pipeline executes the reference trajectory in the target environment and checks the resulting state against the candidate’s verifier. This reveals mismatches among the prompt, initial state, solution, and success criteria.

The negative gate asks: Do relevant incorrect outcomes fail?

Sources indicate that for example, it can mutate parts of the expected outcome and confirm that those states no longer pass verification. This catches weak verifiers that award success without requiring the intended behavior.

Failed candidates go to a critic before being discarded. The critic examines the sample and its failure, looking for inconsistent state, impossible workflows, incorrect task construction, bad reference trajectories, weak verifier logic, or a mismatch with the intended capability. The critic’s findings guide repairs, with a fixed limit on retries:.

In a recent development, A repaired task must pass the relevant checks again. The diagnosis guides repairs to the existing candidate rather than requiring generation to start over.

Sources indicate that passing these checks makes a sample eligible for training, but individually valid samples can still form a repetitive or unbalanced dataset. AutoSynthData therefore also reviews generation at the batch level.

A batch may overrepresent a few easy task families, miss a capability, or reflect too much generation effort spent on a low-yield pattern.

A meta-review examines accepted samples, rejected samples, and generation behavior across each batch. It asks:.

It has been revealed that the controller tracks coverage in the accepted dataset, reduces generation in overrepresented regions, and directs more work toward gaps. When a region repeatedly produces poor candidates, critiques and meta-review guide changes to the generation strategy. These adjustments balance useful learning signal, task quality, coverage, diversity, and low redundancy within the available generation budget and dataset size requirements.

Together, these feedback loops improve both individual tasks and the dataset they form: sample-level checks guide candidate repair, while batch-level review guides future generation.

The useful training distribution changes as the model improves. AutoSynthData treats synthetic data generation as a search for tasks near the target model's capability boundary: difficult enough to expose weaknesses, but solvable enough for the teacher to provide reliable demonstrations.

It has been revealed that after post-training, we evaluate the updated model in the same environment. Tasks it now solves reliably are less useful for the next training round; persistent failures point to capabilities that still need attention. Those results can guide the next generation round.

Sources indicate that our experiments focus on SFT, but the same mechanism could support reinforcement learning (RL): generate tasks that challenge the current policy and provide reliable learning signal, train, then move the generation target with the updated policy. We blueprint to test this moving, difficulty-calibrated frontier beyond SFT.

We use EnterpriseOps Gym to test whether this approach improves a model on tasks in a stateful enterprise environment. We generate training tasks in the Gym’s Hybrid and ITSM environments, fine-tune the target model on accepted samples, and evaluate the resulting checkpoints.

We tested the pipeline on the Hybrid domain of EnterpriseOps Gym using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and Qwen3.8-27B as the teacher.

AutoSynthData generated 2,000 synthetic training samples in about 18 hours. We fine-tuned Gemma on this dataset and evaluated the resulting checkpoints on the benchmark. The best checkpoint was epoch 5.

In a recent development, the synthetic SFT checkpoint improves mean Pass@1 by 7.2 percentage points, a 35% relative improvement, and raises verifier success from 63.01% to 68.55%. It closes 59% of the original Pass@1 gap between Gemma and the reference model.

The training tasks were newly generated from capability specifications; the generator did not receive the original evaluation tasks. The result demonstrates improvement in EnterpriseOps Gym Hybrid, the environment used for this experiment.

According to recent reports, we also applied AutoSynthData to the ITSM domain of EnterpriseOps Gym, using Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it as the target model and DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash as the teacher. AutoSynthData generated 1,994 synthetic training samples in 66 hours. Generation took longer than in the subsequent Hybrid run described above, primarily because the ITSM run used a larger teacher model and preceded pipeline optimizations that improved throughput.

On ITSM, synthetic SFT raises mean Pass@1 from 18.77% to 27.18%, showing that the approach also improves performance in a second domain.

The tasks most useful for training depend on both the environment and the model working in it. AutoSynthData uses the model’s failures to choose what to generate, validates new tasks against the environment, and makes those tasks available for post-training. Our EnterpriseOps Gym results show the value of that approach in a controlled setting. As the model changes, the same process can focus on the gaps that remain.
