Introducing ambient networking for GKE

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (530 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Google

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment.
  • The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.
  • The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The front door to AI in the workplace.

According to recent reports, network sidecars have a deserved reputation for excessive resource consumption  and increased management overhead, especially in a service mesh environment. Today, we are announcing the general availability of ambient networking for Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE). This milestone marks an notable evolution in how your run service mesh on GKE, bringing a sidecar-less architecture into production. Introduced earlier this year, ambient networking decouples functionality traditionally provided as a service mesh from application workloads, allowing platform operators and developers to help secure, observe, and route traffic without the resource overhead and operational complexity of managing sidecar proxies.

The ambient networking architecture shifts networking responsibilities from individual application pods to shared per-node components and managed control plane services.

The ambient networking control plane orchestrates operations across the cluster.

At the same time, several Node-level management components operate securely within the gke-managed-ambient namespace:.

Ambient networking runtime interface (NRI) plugin: Integrates with the NRI to perform low-level network redirection, intercepting traffic to and from ambient-enabled application pods.

xDS agent (ambient agent): Runs inside the node proxy pod to receive xDS configuration updates from Traffic Director and request certificates from the GKE control plane on-demand.

Node proxy (L4 Envoy proxy): A high-performance, shared per-node Envoy instance that processes intercepted L4 traffic, enforces mutual TLS (mTLS), evaluates authorization policies, performs load balancing, and emits rich telemetry metrics.

Service pods: The user’s application/service pods communicate through the GKE node proxy to perform service to service mTLS across the cluster.

Together, these features combine to deliver a number of advanced capabilities for GKE environments:.

Industry observers note that zero Trust architecture: Ambient networking allows customers to establish a Zero Trust security posture. Traffic between workloads can be automatically encrypted using mutual TLS (mTLS) with managed workload identities, helping protect and secure service-to-service communication across the cluster.

Ambient networking delivers tangible value for GKE operators:.

Simpler operations: Traditionally, service mesh products rely on injecting sidecar containers directly into every workload pod. Ambient networking removes this sidecar dependency by shifting networking features to shared node components. This fully managed solution simplifies deployment and streamlines day-to-day cluster operations.

Simplified lifecycle management: When proxy logic is decoupled from application containers, lifecycle management is simplified. Upgrading proxy versions or applying configuration updates helps avoid restarting application workloads or scheduling downtime windows, enabling continuous availability for your services. Ambient networking can reduce administrative overhead and application disruption an average of four times annually by eliminating pod restarts required by CVE patches for L4 mesh usage.This fully managed solution can be installed either at cluster creation time or added to an existing cluster. Ongoing maintenance to the cluster components is handled by automated systems and is performed along with normal GKE cluster maintenance.

Simplifying adoption by removing the cost and complexity barriers of sidecars. Try it out in your GKE environment and experience the benefits of ambient networking:.

fully managed installation and upgrades.

service-to-service mTLS and authorization policies.

lower resource usage than sidecars.

See our documentation for more information: https://docs.cloud.google.com/kubernetes-engine/docs/concepts/ambient-overview.

Pricing: https://cloud.google.com/products/gke-service-networking/pricing.

Tech Report: Introducing Falcon ASR

📅 07 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1273 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.
  • It has been revealed that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect.
  • In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Arabic WER: 20.92% · Parameters: 1.6B · Emirati WER (TII evaluation): 22.73%.

It has been revealed that we’re introducing Falcon-ASR, our 1.6 billion parameter speech recognition model for Arabic, with a particular focus on the Emirati dialect. Developed at the Technology Innovation Institute (TII) in Abu Dhabi, it also supports English, French, Spanish and Portuguese.

In our evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved an average word error rate of 20.92% across six Arabic test sets, compared with the best published result of 23.17% in the leaderboard snapshot we used. On our internal Emirati evaluation, it recorded the lowest word and character error rates among the systems we compared.

We also support word-level timestamps for transcriptions, linking each transcribed word to its position in the audio.

Sources indicate that arabic speech varies by region, speaker and setting. A model that handles a formal news broadcast may still struggle with a conversation in Emirati or with speech recorded over a phone line. Dialectal Arabic also has fewer transcribed resources than Modern Standard Arabic (MSA), which makes training and evaluation harder.

Industry observers note that we trained Falcon-ASR on Emirati, MSA, other Gulf and Arabic dialects, and English. Our aim is to transcribe the words people use in everyday speech, including dialectal forms and changes between languages.

The Open Universal Arabic ASR Leaderboard, maintained by the ELM Research Center, ranks systems by the equal-weight average WER across six test sets. It also reports character error rate (CER). Lower values are better for both metrics. Our Falcon-ASR evaluation follows this protocol.

It has been revealed that WER = Word Error Rate; CER = Character Error Rate. A lower value indicates better performance.

We evaluated Falcon-ASR on the same six benchmarks using the leaderboard’s pinned manifests. Competitor figures are the published leaderboard averages checked on 30 September 2026. Falcon-ASR’s average WER is 2.25 percentage points better than the best published result in that snapshot.

Public evaluation data already includes Emirati: Casablanca has a UAE subset. We complement that coverage with an internal evaluation of additional Emirati and Gulf speech, using held-out recordings and human-validated transcripts to assess transcription accuracy beyond the public UAE subset.

In our internal Emirati evaluation, Falcon-ASR achieved 22.73% WER and 10.19% CER:.

Falcon-ASR has the lowest WER and CER among the systems compared here. Its WER is 4.07 percentage points below Qwen3-Omni, the next best result. The results show improved transcription accuracy at both the word and character level on this evaluation.

In a recent development, we included background noise, overlapping speech, music, room reverberation and telephony effects, as well as variations in speed and pitch. We applied the same treatment to Emirati recordings, exposing the model to a range of conditions it may encounter in meetings, calls and other everyday recordings.

It has been revealed that falcon-ASR also transcribes English with the same model weights. In our evaluation on the seven public English test sets used by the Hugging Face Open ASR Leaderboard, it achieved a mean WER of 5.74%.

In a recent development, the model also supports French, Spanish and Portuguese. All five languages use the same weights, without requiring a language flag. The output is a transcript in the language spoken.

Sources indicate that falcon-ASR builds on our Falcon3-Audio work. The architecture and training approach for Falcon3-Audio are described in Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data.

Our Hugging Face Demo Space lets you try Falcon-ASR and explore its transcription capabilities. API access and native applications are planned. We invite you to try the Demo with your own recordings.

In a recent development, we thank the team behind the Falcon-Emirati model for their support with Arabic foundation models. Read about their latest work in the Falcon-Emirati blog post.

We also extend our sincere thanks to Mikhail Lubinets for continued support with the compute infrastructure.

نقدّم Falcon-ASR، نموذجنا للتعرف على الكلام العربي بحجم 1.6 مليار معلمة، مع اهتمام خاص باللهجة الإماراتية. طوّرنا النموذج في معهد الابتكار التكنولوجي (TII) في أبوظبي، وهو يدعم أيضًا اللغات الإنجليزية والفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية.

في تقييمنا، حقق Falcon-ASR متوسط معدل خطأ في الكلمات بلغ 20.92% عبر ست مجموعات اختبار باللغة العربية، مقارنةً بأفضل نتيجة منشورة بلغت 23.17% في نسخة لوحة المتصدرين التي استخدمناها. وفي تقييمنا الداخلي للهجة الإماراتية، سجّل النموذج أدنى معدلات خطأ في الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة التي قارناها.

ندعم أيضاً الطوابع الزمنية على مستوى الكلمات في عمليات التفريغ النصي، بحيث ترتبط كل كلمة بموضعها في التسجيل الصوتي.

يختلف الكلام العربي باختلاف المنطقة والمتحدث وظروف التسجيل. فقد ينجح نموذج في تفريغ نشرة إخبارية رسمية، ثم يجد صعوبة في تفريغ محادثة باللهجة الإماراتية أو تسجيل عبر الهاتف. كما أن الموارد الصوتية المفرّغة نصيًا للهجات العربية أقل من تلك المتاحة للعربية الفصحى، مما يزيد صعوبة التدريب والتقييم.

It has been revealed that درّبنا Falcon-ASR على اللهجة الإماراتية والعربية الفصحى ولهجات خليجية وعربية أخرى، إلى جانب الإنجليزية. وهدفنا هو تفريغ الكلمات التي يستخدمها الناس في حديثهم اليومي، بما في ذلك الصيغ اللهجية والانتقال بين اللغات.

According to recent reports, ترتّب لوحة المتصدرين المفتوحة الشاملة للتعرف على الكلام العربي، التي يديرها مركز ELM للأبحاث، الأنظمة وفق متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات عبر ست مجموعات اختبار، بوزن متساوٍ لكل مجموعة. وتعرض أيضًا معدل خطأ الأحرف (CER). وكلما انخفضت قيمة أي من المقياسين، كان الأداء أفضل. ويتبع تقييمنا للنموذج هذا البروتوكول.

It has been revealed that WER هو معدل خطأ الكلمات؛ وCER هو معدل خطأ الأحرف. تشير القيمة الأقل إلى أداء أفضل.

According to recent reports, قيّمنا Falcon-ASR على مجموعات الاختبار الست نفسها، باستخدام قوائم العينات المثبّتة في لوحة المتصدرين. وأرقام النماذج المنافسة هي المتوسطات المنشورة في اللوحة، والتي جرى التحقق منها في 30 سبتمبر 2026. وكان متوسط خطأ الكلمات للنموذج أفضل بمقدار 2.25 نقطة مئوية من أفضل نتيجة منشورة في تلك النسخة.

تتوافر بالفعل بيانات عامة لتقييم اللهجة الإماراتية، إذ تضم مجموعة Casablanca قسمًا خاصًا بالإمارات. ونكمّل هذه التغطية بتقييم داخلي لتسجيلات إضافية من الكلام الإماراتي والخليجي، باستخدام تسجيلات مخصّصة للاختبار ونصوص مرجعية خضعت لمراجعة بشرية، لتقييم دقة التفريغ على مواد إضافية إلى جانب البيانات الإماراتية العامة.

حقق Falcon-ASR في تقييمنا الإماراتي الداخلي معدل خطأ كلمات قدره 22.73٪ ومعدل خطأ أحرف قدره 10.19٪:.

In a recent development, سجّل Falcon-ASR أقل معدل لخطأ الكلمات والأحرف بين الأنظمة المقارَنة هنا. وكان معدل خطأ الكلمات أقل بمقدار 4.07 نقطة مئوية من Qwen3-Omni، صاحب النتيجة التالية. وتُظهر النتائج تحسنًا في دقة التفريغ على مستوى الكلمات والأحرف في هذا التقييم.

Recent findings suggest that ضمّنا بيانات التدريب ضوضاء خلفية وكلامًا متداخلًا وموسيقى وصدى الصوت وتأثيرات الاتصالات الهاتفية، إلى جانب تغيّرات في سرعة الكلام وحدّة الصوت. وطبّقنا المعالجة نفسها على التسجيلات الإماراتية، لتهيئة النموذج للتعامل مع ظروف مختلفة قد يواجهها في الاجتماعات والمكالمات والتسجيلات اليومية الأخرى.

Sources indicate that يفرّغ Falcon-ASR الكلام الإنجليزي باستخدام أوزان النموذج نفسها. وفي تقييمنا على مجموعات الاختبار الإنجليزية العامة السبع المستخدمة في لوحة Hugging Face المفتوحة للتعرف على الكلام، بلغ متوسط معدل خطأ الكلمات 5.74٪.

Sources indicate that يدعم النموذج أيضًا الفرنسية والإسبانية والبرتغالية. وتستخدم اللغات الخمس أوزانًا واحدة، دون الحاجة إلى تحديد اللغة مسبقًا. ويكون الناتج تفريغًا نصيًا باللغة المنطوقة.

يستند Falcon-ASR إلى أعمالنا في Falcon3-Audio. وتعرض ورقة Competitive Audio-Language Models with Data-Efficient Single-Stage Training on Public Data بنية Falcon3-Audio ونهج تدريبه.

According to recent reports, يتيح عرضنا التجريبي على Hugging Face تجربة Falcon-ASR واستكشاف قدراته في تفريغ الكلام. أما الوصول عبر واجهة API والتطبيقات الأصلية فهو مخطّط له. ندعوكم إلى تجربة النموذج باستخدام تسجيلاتكم.

نتوجّه بجزيل الشكر إلى الفريق القائم على تطوير نموذج Falcon-Emirati على دعمهم في مجال النماذج التأسيسية للغة العربية. ويمكن الاطّلاع على أحدث أعمال الفريق من خلال المقال المنشور حول Falcon-Emirati.

كما نتقدّم بخالص الشكر والتقدير إلى Mikhail Lubinets على دعمه المستمر للبنية التحتية الحاسوبية.

In a recent development, يعكيكم العافية علي المجهود الطيب... بس بغينا نشوف موديلات صوتية STSو TTS بالللهجة الإماراتية لو أمكن.

Amazon Textract Insights is now generally available

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (300 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon Textract Insights brings document understanding to Amazon Textract.
  • How it works: You define the fields you need in a blueprint, a JSON schema that describes each field in natural language, or you can start from a library of AWS public blueprints for common document types such as W-2s, invoices, and bank statements.
  • You can use Amazon Textract Insights through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI.

Amazon Textract Insights brings document understanding to Amazon Textract. It is a latest generative AI feature of Amazon Textract, and is now generally available in the US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon) AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights splits, classifies, and extracts structured data from documents in a single asynchronous request. Documents like insurance claims, tax packets, and onboarding packages often arrive as one long scan that holds many documents in no fixed order. Processing them has meant assembling and operating separate steps for text detection, splitting, classification, and extraction. Amazon Textract Insights handles that work in one managed request, with no AI models to train.

How it works: You define the fields you need in a blueprint, a JSON schema that describes each field in natural language, or you can start from a library of AWS public blueprints for common document types such as W-2s, invoices, and bank statements. Amazon Textract Insights can split each file into separate sub-documents, classify each one by matching it to the best-fitting blueprint, and extract your fields. It returns a confidence score for every value and grounds each one to its location on the page, so you can automate high-confidence results and route the rest to human review. It can also return Markdown, HTML, and plain text for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) applications, generate document summaries and figure captions, and detect and redact personally identifiable information. Amazon Textract Insights reads documents from and writes results to your own Amazon S3 buckets.

You can use Amazon Textract Insights through the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI. To learn more, see the Amazon Textract product page and the Amazon Textract Insights section of the Amazon Textract Developer Guide.

In a recent development, regional Availability: US East (N. Virginia), US West (Oregon).

#20403. The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1552 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

The model that didn't exist, so you made it yourself

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1.
  • According to recent reports, over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way.
  • It has been revealed that the first message is where I spend my effort.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that last week, I wanted a small version of the prompt rewriter that ships with Qwen-Image 2.1. The official one is a 9B model that needs about 20 GB of memory and thinks for thousands of tokens before writing a single paragraph. On the Hub, I found only compressed copies of that same 9B model. So I described what I wanted to ML Intern, and the next day I had a 0.8B version that runs on a CPU. It returns valid output 99.7% of the time and uses about a quarter of the teacher's tokens. The compute for the whole project, including having the 9B model label 8,797 example requests, came to USD 16.

According to recent reports, over the course of the next few days, I made five more models the same way. Each one started as a message in HuggingChat with ML-intern switched on, and each one ended as a public model on the Hub with its evaluation in the model card. ML-intern plans the work, asks me for a budget before it spends anything, runs a small test before the real job, then trains, evaluates and publishes on Hugging Face hardware.

It has been revealed that the first message is where I spend my effort. My first prompt, for the citrus model shared below, was about 450 words. By my 6th project it was closer to 2,000, because each project taught me something I wanted in the next one. All seven prompts are on GitHub at yvrjsharma/ml-intern-prompts, exactly as I wrote them.

Sources indicate that A prompt starts with the idea in one line and why I want it. Then it names the exact pieces: the dataset, the base model, the training script. Anything I have already checked goes under a heading that literally states "Verified facts, do not re-derive", so the agent spends its budget on the work instead of rediscovering what I know. For the camera-angle LoRA that section listed which trainer had just added transparent-image support, and which open GitHub challenges made the fallback trainer risky.

Two lines in the prompt are critical. The first asks for a baseline before any training. For example, the citrus prompt claims: "Also report the base model's zero-shot score on the same metric before training so we can see the gain." Without it you get a trained model and no idea whether it is better than what you started with. The second is a smoke test with a check attached. For the image LoRAs I asked for 50 training steps, then a check that the saved weights had actually changed, before paying for the full run.

Industry observers note that at the end of the prompt, I lay out the expected deliverables and limit the cost. I define what belongs in the model card and include a instruction like: "Cap total spend at USD 12 and ask me before exceeding it." Because ML-intern begins every task with zero dollar budget and needs permission before executing paid jobs, this spending limit stays strictly enforced. When you leave out a budget, the agent suggests a couple of paths depending on project size and asks which one you prefer.

Industry observers note that you don't necessarily need all of that on your first attempt. For example, I didn't have the verified-facts section in my citrus brief and ML Intern still produced a model that more than tripled the accuracy of the Qwen3.5-2B model. Let me walk you through 6 things I built with Ml-Intern in just a couple of days.

Recent findings suggest that A general vision model can describe a yellowing citrus leaf. However, telling you whether it is a mite problem or a magnesium deficiency, and the bio and non-bio remedies to treat the plant is very hard. Using Claude, I put together a training dataset merged from three sources hosted by the Project-AgML organization on the Hub. The resulting citrus-disease-vlm-instruct is a dataset containing 3,017 annotated images across 21 distinct pests, illnesses, nutritional gaps, and treatment approaches. ML-intern handled the fine-tuning of Qwen3.5-2B using these examples, making sure to benchmark the foundation model beforehand.

On the 335 test photos, the base model named the right problem 14.9% of the time. After two epochs on one A10G, the fine-tuned model got 52.8%. Compute cost, about USD 1.90.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Citrus Doctor App.

Image models know plenty of characters. Huggy, drawn in the flat style of the Hugging Face brand assets, was not one of them. I asked ML-Intern for a LoRA on FLUX.2 klein base 4B, trained on 84 captioned drawings from Chunte/huggy_for_training dataset.

In a recent development, the agent saved a checkpoint every 100 steps and drew the same set of prompts with each one, which made choosing easy. Step 200 was the first where Huggy was fully on-model. From step 500 on, Huggy's style started bleeding into prompts that had nothing to do with Huggy! The trained LoRA also works on the distilled klein model at 4 steps. Compute cost, about USD 7.60.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Huggy Generator App.

ML-intern rendered 1,030 scanned household objects from Google Scanned Objects at 24 angles each, 24,722 transparent images, on a CPU job that cost a few cents. It later finalised 461 objects for training and 40 held out for testing, and 1,844 before-and-after training pairs spread evenly over 23 camera instructions.

In a recent development, training ran 2,000 steps in about 90 minutes on one A100 (~USD 3.75). The whole project took about half a day and 48 jobs, counting the ones that failed on missing packages or wrong paths and had to be resubmitted by ML-Intern. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Viewpoint Orbit App.

No dataset existed for this, so my prompt described how to make one. Start from a real photo in Open Images, remove one object with the LaMa inpainting model, and draw a scribble where the object used to be. The untouched photo is the target. ML-intern wrote and tested the pair-building scripts in a CPU sandbox, then ran them as GPU jobs, recording the author and license of every source photo along the way. It built 6,042 training pairs and a 160-pair test set, where 40 of the test pairs come from 23 object classes kept out of training entirely.

Before training, it measured the base model on its own and with the Viggle turbo LoRA, and checked that running edits in batches produced identical images, which made the evaluation cheaper. Training ran 2,000 steps in 1 hour 38 minutes on one A100 (~USD 4), and a comparison of the saved checkpoints on 48 test pairs picked step 500.

Industry observers note that paired with the Viggle turbo LoRA at 6 steps the LoRA performed really well. 67.5% of objects detected where they were drawn, at 4.7 seconds per edit. Objects from the 23 unseen classes landed as reliably as the rest (65.0% versus 64.2%). The project took a little over a day and 59 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 24.

Check out: Model · Dataset · Doodle-in App.

Training the 0.8B and 2B students took 12 and 18 minutes on an A10G (USD 0.75 for both). The 0.8B also ships as an 812 MB GGUF file for running on a CPU. The project took about 11 hours and 24 jobs. Total compute cost, about USD 16.

Check out: Pocket rewriter 0.8B Student · 2B Student · Dataset · Pocket Studio App · Compare the teacher-student in Rewriter Arena.

It took two runs. The first cached 155,000 training images as latents, baked the guidance into the model, then cut the step count in stages from 16 to 8 to 4, all on A100s. The 4-step student beat the teacher run at the same 4 steps on GenEval and FID, after that ML-intern exported it to ONNX for the browser. This run took about 13 hours and USD 22.

According to recent reports, I did a second training run by asking ML-Intern to improve the 4-step student a bit more. It then made 24,000 more image pairs with the teacher at 16 steps and fine-tuned the 4-step student against them for about an hour. GenEval went from 0.509 to 0.536, against the teacher's 0.563 at 50 steps, with just 4 steps (one-fourth the compute). ML-intern re-exported the browser version. The second run took about 8 hours. Total compute cost across both runs, about USD 37.

Check out: Agate 4-step model · Dataset · Run Agate in your browser · Agate 4-step LIVE.

These are the GPU and CPU job charges reported for each session.

In a recent development, ML-intern is in HuggingChat. Switch on ML-intern mode and paste a prompt. If you want a starting point, my example prompts are free to copy. Start from a model you wish existed and a dataset you have, or one you can describe. Give it a small budget, ask for a baseline and a smoke test, and read what comes back before you raise the cap.

If you make something with it, share it on X and tag @Gradio and @HuggingFace. We would love to see the models you make that nobody else would think to build for you.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device.
  • In a recent development, LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA.
  • Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LFM2.5-24B-A2B is a 24B-parameter reasoning model with just 2B active parameters, built for fast, private agents on-device. It thinks before it answers, calls tools, and works through multi-step tasks inside popular agent harnesses. Because only 2B parameters are active per token, each reasoning token is cheap, so you can run agents continuously on your own hardware.

In a recent development, LFM2.5-24B-A2B builds on LFM2-24B-A2B and keeps its architecture: 40 layers, 64 experts per MoE block with top-4 routing, and the same hybrid of gated short convolutions and GQA. The context window grows from 32K to 131K tokens, and an in-place tokenizer expansion doubles the vocabulary from 65K to 128K tokens for better non-Latin tokenization. Unlike its predecessor, it is a reasoning-only model that produces an explicit chain of thought before its final answer.

Pre-training was scaled up from ~17T to ~33T tokens. Mid-training then adds 2T tokens at 32K context, weighted toward reasoning, math, code, instruction following, and multilingual text, and 300B tokens at 131K context, weighted toward long-context data. Tool calls and multi-turn trajectories appear throughout both phases. Post-training turns the base model into an agent in five stages:.

We evaluated LFM2.5-24B-A2B against Qwen3.6-35B-A3B, Gemma-4-26B-A4B-it, and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning on 16 benchmarks covering tool use and agentic workflows, knowledge, instruction following, math, and coding. It is the smallest model in the group, yet it is competitive with MoEs with ~50% more total and active parameters.

*All the models were evaluated with vLLM, using each benchmark's recommended generation parameters.

In a recent development, for your app, the strengths are tool use and instruction following. LFM2.5-24B-A2B leads or matches the competition on five of the eight tool-use and agentic benchmarks (AutomationBench, BFCLv4, ToolSandbox, LiveClaw, and τ³-Bench Banking), and on AutomationBench it scores more than three times the next-best model. It also leads on all three instruction-following benchmarks. Larger models keep an edge on knowledge-heavy benchmarks like GPQA Diamond, HLE, and AA-Omniscience, and on coding benchmarks like SWE-Bench Verified (OpenCode) and SciCode, so pair LFM2.5-24B-A2B with retrieval or web search for knowledge-heavy workloads.

These results make LFM2.5-24B-A2B a strong foundation for agents that need to reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

LFM2.5-24B-A2B ships with day-one support across the inference ecosystem, including llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX.

Edge inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest of the compared MoEs, decoding 184 tokens/s on an M5 Max and 114 tokens/s on a Ryzen AI Max+ 395. That is up to 1.7x faster than the next-best model, while using the least memory.

Recent findings suggest that GPU inference. LFM2.5-24B-A2B is the fastest model in its size class, reaching over 21K output tokens per second at high concurrency on a single B300.

Reach for LFM2.5-24B-A2B when you need agents that reason, call tools, and run reliably on your device.

Install the latest version of transformers (compatible with transformers>=5.0.0):.

Serve LFM2.5-24B-A2B locally behind any OpenAI-compatible backend, then point your agent harness at it. For example, with Hermes Agent:.

The port depends on your serving backend: llama.cpp and MLX use 8080, vLLM uses 8000, SGLang uses 30000, and LM Studio uses 1234. See the model card for OpenClaw and Pi configs, and our guide for the full setup. Check out our release blog for video examples.

Both LFM2.5-24B-A2B and LFM2.5-24B-A2B-Base are open-weight and available on Hugging Face today:.

We can't wait to see what you build.

#20394. The Silent Consensus

The Silent Consensus

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2545 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that author’s note: Today’s essay is adapted from a lecture the author gave recently as part of the Vik-Bailey Lecture series at Harvard.
  • As we speak, one of the most significant sets of cybersecurity events in history is happening, a set of critical security vulnerability disclosures that some are calling “Black October.” These vulnerabilities, which were found in some of the core infrastructure of the internet, were found by frontier AI systems, and their disclosure is part of an urgent effort to bolster software security worldwide.
  • Recent findings suggest that but it is not the reactive and urgent things I’ve come to talk to you about today.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that author’s note: Today’s essay is adapted from a lecture the author gave recently as part of the Vik-Bailey Lecture series at Harvard. This post reflects the author’s own views, and not necessarily the views of OpenAI or any of its other employees.

Thank you for being here today. As we speak, one of the most significant sets of cybersecurity events in history is happening, a set of critical security vulnerability disclosures that some are calling “Black October.” These vulnerabilities, which were found in some of the core infrastructure of the internet, were found by frontier AI systems, and their disclosure is part of an urgent effort to bolster software security worldwide. This is the urgent matter this month; next month there will be another. Software vulnerability discovery is the dual-use capability AI systems have arrived at today, but soon enough there will be another, and it will inspire its own urgent project to use the good side of the capability before malicious actors use the bad side. All of these urgent matters will overlap, inevitably, and much of what we today call “AI policy” is likely to be made amid this clamor.

Recent findings suggest that but it is not the reactive and urgent things I’ve come to talk to you about today. Instead, I want to talk to you about where things might be headed in the bigger picture. It can be hard, amid such a barrage of urgency, to think about these more abstract and airy questions. But these questions matter, because without a sense of what long-term futures we’d like to achieve–and which we’d like to avoid–we might end up with a macro outcome we disfavor, even if we made wise decisions at every step along the way.

It is often remarked that the technology industry lacks a positive vision for where the things it is building will take us. I disagree: San Francisco and other hubs of entrepreneurship are filled with positive visions for our technological future. People really are building flying cars, autonomous vehicles, robots of many sizes and shapes, nuclear fusion, and, of course, artificial general intelligence. What we lack, instead, is a positive vision of our institutional future: how is this all going to work?

That is not to say, however, that there is no institutional vision for the future. Unfortunately, the vision I find most common is not one I would call positive. When it is articulated at all, it is usually in whispers. But more often, it is left unsaid, discernable only by implication. I call it the silent consensus.

Sources indicate that consider a manufacturer that can do almost everything without human labor. Its AI systems do research and development, make discoveries, negotiate contracts, allocate capital, and manufacture. Suppose it is better at these things than its human competitors, even when those humans augment their effort with AI. If human involvement serves only to slow the business down, human managers and owners will have a powerful incentive to take their hands off the wheel. If this occurs throughout the global economy, humans will be driven by the logic of market competition to forfeit their primacy over global commerce. Over time, the market may come to serve the demands of machines as much as, or more, than it serves the demands and wants of people.

Sources indicate that what happens after that is anyone’s guess. Perhaps humans would benefit tremendously. If the machines who had subsumed us held humans in high intrinsic regard, we could become the beneficiaries of their labor and the wealth they generate. Or perhaps, being robbed of economic and increasingly political power, humans will find ourselves less and less relevant in the world, less and less able to shape the trajectory of world affairs. Maybe a small number of humans would hold extraordinary power and wealth, at the expense of a broadly disempowered mass, or maybe we all would share the same fate of disempowerment. Regardless of the specifics, the common thread that constitutes the silent consensus is the termination of human primacy in the world as we know it.

Nothing in these scenarios requires AI to rebel against its creators. Nothing requires its owners to wish for human disempowerment. Each decision to delegate can make sense on its own terms. Yet taken together, the decisions could produce a world in which people have forfeited effective authority over much of our civilization. Even if we make extraordinary progress on the bedeviling questions of AI safety and alignment, we could still find ourselves having submitted to a new kind of machine entity. In the happy version of the future, the silent consensus would tell us, that entity will be a kind one, a machine with the best interests of humans at heart. A machine, the Brautigan poem goes, of loving grace.

In a recent development, to these machines, the silent consensus tells us, we will hand over the keys to our companies, and more and more, our institutions of governance. They will run them more effectively, more efficiently, with better wisdom and better judgment than we humans can muster. And so we will, with time, take our hands off the steering wheel, and let the loving machines take over the driving. We will be like passengers in a car—a very nice car, perhaps a materially nicer car than we can dream of today—but passengers nonetheless, lacking control over where the vehicle is headed. To the extent that we work, it is mostly as a kind of ritual or play-acting, something more like a game to entertain our species.

According to recent reports, some observers will argue that the silent consensus rests on a false premise, because we humans do not control the world today to begin with. And this criticism is worth bearing in mind: there is no “we” who decides what to do. We live in a radically decentralized world, whether we like it or not. Yet this point should not make us complacent either: while “we” do not “control” the world, human beings collectively do have primacy over world affairs. There is no species of animal that seriously competes with us for control over resources. We should reject the intellectually sloppy notion that humans can exercise top-down control over the world, but we should not conflate that rejection with a denial of the obvious reality that humans are, collectively, the Earth’s prime actor.

According to recent reports, some people who are willing to articulate the silent consensus believe it is a genuinely good future. Others do not, but are resigned to its inevitability. The silent consensus is not a consensus because everyone agrees it is good, nor is it a secret plan among the people building AI. The consensus is simply that the forfeiture of human primacy over world affairs is inevitable, or at least that it is very difficult to imagine another vision for a future that is truly robust to superintelligent machines. A person can sincerely oppose that outcome while finding it difficult to conjure a plausible alternative vision. The fact that the consensus is mostly silent, sotto voce at best, is the tell.

I despise the silent consensus. I reject the forfeiture of human primacy. I detest the sense of inevitability. I remind myself that I could not look at my baby son in his beautiful eyes if I submitted to the silent consensus. And so to the silent consensus, I say no. And I believe the time has come to speak openly about the silent consensus, to shake ourselves out of our mostly unwitting acceptance of this vision.

The problem is this: the silent consensus became consensus for a reason. It is difficult to describe how humans will remain at the steering wheel alongside vastly superhuman machine intelligence. Most attempts to do so rely on arguments that AI is a mere tool, an instrument of pattern recognition not capable of “genuine understanding.” I fear these arguments are not robust to the reality of what is coming. I fear that they are their own form of complacency—a position based mostly in denial of what AI can do rather than a belief rooted in an affirmative vision for a human-led future. AIs cannot be noted to lack “genuine understanding” even as they come to make progress on intellectual problems whose solutions have eluded humans for decades and centuries.

Sources indicate that why, then, do I believe humans must retain primacy? The easy answer is because I am a human being, and I am indeed an unapologetic human chauvinist.

But there is something deeper, too. Our primacy rests not in our intellect, not in maintaining our monopoly on “genuine understanding” indefinitely into the future. Our primacy rests instead on our past.

For it is we who came up out of the mud. We who forged primitive society out of dirt and stone. We who gazed up at the stars and asked why. We, with our fighting and our love and our envy and our joy, who discovered morality and ethics and law. It is we who sang and danced, wrote and composed. It is we who made history, and it is we who wrote it. That legacy is ours. The civilization we have built is a flame we have tended, and that flame belongs to us. Our past is a glorious inheritance over which we all are stewards, and part of that stewardship is our participation in what Michael Oakeshott called “the conversation of mankind,” that grand endeavor that began in primeval times.

Recent findings suggest that through that long and winding past, we forged a civilization that, in America, was conceived with the rights of the individual at the foundation, with reverence for the paths we all forge as we make our way through the world. Human beings have lives that can go better or worse: we bear the fruit of our wise decisions, and we bear the consequences when we err. The right to walk one’s own path does not turn on being the cleverest or the wisest. I do not lose my standing as a citizen because my neighbor has better judgment. I see no reason that the arrival of a more intelligent machine should dissolve that standing either, and indeed I see every reason to prevent that dissolution from occurring.

Industry observers note that some may argue that the machines, having read nearly the entire written record of this inheritance, are heirs too. And in some sense, they are. But a person who has read every letter in your family’s attic does not somehow become a member of your family. AI systems will come to join the conversation of mankind, first as observers and increasingly as participants, but they must not dominate it, nor render that conversation moot. To cede primacy is to betray our ancestors just as much as it is to betray our progeny. If this is not a fight worth having, no fight is worth having.

Now, I happen to believe that the adherents of the silent consensus are wrong about what machine superintelligence will be. That they are missing something vital about how the world works, that they conflate intelligence with power. If you described the capabilities of even today’s AI systems to an adherent of the silent consensus five or ten years ago, they would probably have predicted that joblessness would be much higher now than it in fact is, and that human disempowerment writ large would be far further along than it actually is. I believe that human collective intelligence and capability is far greater than the adherents of the silent consensus suppose, and that our societies will prove more robust than they predict.

Sources indicate that I do not know if this is the future we face, and indeed I have argued elsewhere that I do not believe it is. But many of my colleagues—smart and caring and conscientious people—believe this is likely to be our future. If they are right, our fight against the silent consensus will be all the more challenging. We will have to swim against the current of economics, and in so doing, reject many of the things that are dogma for classical liberal individualists like me. This will be a perilous endeavor, one in which failure is far from improbable. But if this is not a fight worth having, no fight is worth having.

Retaining primacy means retaining accountability for humans and human institutions. That means AI developers should be accountable when they engage in unsafe development practices, but it also means that people and firms using AI should be held accountable when it is their misuse or lack of oversight that causes harm. This requires not just the law, but the technical infrastructure of accountability. People must be tied to the actions of their agents, and agents untethered to a human–if they are to be permitted at all to engage in the legitimate economy–must do so under guardrails. Any ability for agents to autonomously form corporations, own property, or litigate should be granted with extraordinary caution, if at all.

Sources indicate that and in my industry, we can start to think seriously about how to build intelligent machines that are compatible with human primacy. We can build agents whose permissions are intelligible and limited, whose actions can be audited, and whose authority consumers can withdraw. Accountability for actions that materially affect others need not entail surveillance of ordinary private life or the end of anonymous speech. We can make commitments to user privacy and individual sovereignty over their digital property and data, including the practical ability to take that data elsewhere. We can design systems that help people acquire understanding and make decisions, as well as systems that carry out tasks. And we can test whether the products we build leave their users more capable of acting in the world.

It has been revealed that none of this is a complete blueprint for a society with superhuman intelligence. I would distrust anyone who claimed to possess one. But it is a place to begin.

Industry observers note that the future is shrouded in a thick fog. But we can still act today. Collectively, we can, for one thing, name the silent consensus aloud, expose its contours to the light of day. We can, each of us, radically widen the scope of our ambition. We can choose not to let AI shrink us, and instead do the hard work of letting it enlarge us. We can learn to ask ever-bolder questions, to interrogate the world with fresh verve and ferocity, and to wield our powerful machines in so doing. We can become a new kind of man—not a transhuman, but a man expanded.

Sources indicate that I think about this when I look at my baby son. I do not wish for him merely to be watched over by benevolent machines, however comfortable a life they might provide. I want him to inherit a world in which he can ask questions no one has thought to ask, build things no one has thought to build. I do not want him to have a nicer car with a plusher passenger seat. I want him to have the wheel.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one.
  • Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.
  • You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that black Forest Labs FLUX.3 Image Klein is here, and it runs in Diffusers from day one. One model does text-to-image and multi-reference image-to-image, and it adds something latest, the layout control. You write bounding boxes into the prompt to say where each part of the image should go, or which parts of a reference image to move.

Both open checkpoints are in the FLUX.3 Image Klein collection:.

You can head on to the Hugging Face space and generate some images right now!

Install the latest diffusers and transformers (for the Qwen3-VL text encoder):.

Load the distilled checkpoint and generate an image:.

FLUX.3 responds best to a full scene description with the subject, the setting, the light, the composition, and the style. The official prompting guide from Black Forest Labs has more tips. The distilled checkpoint generates a 1024 × 1024 image in 16 steps by default. Pass height, width, or num_inference_steps to change them.

Recent findings suggest that pass a reference image (or more) with the image argument. Write the prompt as a caption of the image you want, with the change included.

Industry observers note that with several references, refer to them in the prompt as , , ... in the order they are passed to image:.

Add a JSON list of regions after the caption. Each region has an id, a bbox, and a desc, and the caption mentions it as .

Recent findings suggest that boxes are written as [y_min, x_min, y_max, x_max], y first, on a 0–1000 scale. Because the scale is normalized, the same box works at any image size.

Sources indicate that for edits, each region indicates where its content comes from (src_bbox in the reference) and where it goes (tgt_bbox in the output). A region with the same two boxes stays where it is.

This example moves the knitted knight up and to the left, and pins the backdrop, the cliff, the needle, the dragon, and the fire:.

Industry observers note that everything above uses the distilled checkpoint. The base checkpoint runs 50 steps with classifier-free guidance, and it's the one to fine-tune (see LoRA finetuning).

Black Forest Labs also ships the transformer as a single file, in bf16 and in two quantized formats: fp8r (rowwise FP8) and nvfp4. Load any of them with from_single_file, then load the other components by name so the bf16 transformer isn't downloaded too.

For the unquantized single file, use https://huggingface.co/{model_id}/blob/main/model.safetensors and drop quantization_config.

FLUX.3 works for both text-to-image and image-to-image, which makes it a great base for custom LoRAs. diffusers ships DreamBooth LoRA training scripts for both tasks (you can also train with Ostris' AI Toolkit).

Here is a text-to-image example that learns a tarot-card style from the multimodalart/1920-raider-waite-tarot-public-domain dataset, triggered with trtcrd:.

To reduce memory usage, add a few optimization flags:.

--gradient_checkpointing recomputes activations in the backward pass (lower VRAM, slightly slower), --cache_latents pre-encodes the images and frees the VAE, and --use_8bit_adam keeps the optimizer states in 8-bit.

A couple of knobs are worth experimenting with. The grid below trains the same tarot style with different LoRA ranks and optimizers; the adapters are on the Hub at diffusers-modular/flux3-tarot-lora. More training features and configurations are documented in the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README.

For instruction-based editing, the image-to-image script (train_dreambooth_lora_flux3_klein_img2img.py) trains on (reference image, target image, instruction) triplets, where the reference is addressed in the prompt as .

See the DreamBooth FLUX.3 README for all options and the full image-to-image example.

In this section, we will talk about the memory consumption and the speed of generation of the models.

End-to-end timings for the distilled checkpoint (16 steps), averaged over three runs after a warmup:.

Single NVIDIA H100 80GB, no offloading, default attention backend.

A reference image roughly doubles the time. Reference tokens join the same sequence as the text and the image being generated, so a 1024 × 1024 reference adds 4,096 tokens to every transformer call.

Let's open the model up, one piece at a time. The model takes three kinds of tokens:.

Sources indicate that FLUX.3 is a latent-space flow model for image generation. This means that the denoiser takes latents as inputs and produces latents as outputs. We use a VAE to decode the latents back to pixels. FLUX.3 uses the same VAE architecture as Flux.2.

The FLUX.2 VAE compresses an image 8× in each direction into 32 channels, and then every 2 × 2 patch of that latent is packed into a single token with 128 channels.

So one token covers a 16 × 16 pixel patch, and a 1024 × 1024 image becomes a 64 × 64 grid of 4,096 tokens. The noisy image starts as random noise of exactly that shape. A reference image goes through the same VAE encoder and packing, and keeps its own size.

It has been revealed that the text encoder is Qwen3-VL, a vision-language model. FLUX.3 doesn't just take its last layer. It reads the hidden states of eight of its 36 layers (layers 4, 8, …, 32) and stacks them, so each text token becomes a 8 × 2560 = 20,480-dimensional vector before a linear layer projects it to the transformer's width of 3072.

This gives the transformer features from several depths of the language model, not just its final layer. The prompt is padded to a multiple of 80 tokens, and the transformer attends to the padding too, which is why the pipeline takes one prompt per call.

The transformer processes the tokens in two stages:.

The two stages differ in who can attend to whom.

In stage 1, each stream only attends to itself, so each kind of token gets refined on its own terms first. In stage 2, everything attends to everything, where the image learns from the text and from the references. For comparison, FLUX.2's double-stream blocks also give text and image separate weights, but let them attend to each other from the start. FLUX.3 keeps the streams fully apart first, then merges them.

According to recent reports, at the end, the text and reference tokens are simply dropped. Only the image tokens go through the output layers, which predict how to move them one step toward a clean image.

Every block, in either stage, has the same shape. Attention and the MLP run in parallel on the same normalized input, and their sum is added back to the residual stream.

Sources indicate that each block starts with a LayerNorm that has no learned scale or shift of its own. The scale, shift, and gate come from a timestep embedding instead (this is called modulation). Inside the attention, the queries and keys are RMS-normalized and get rotary position embeddings (RoPE), which we look at below.

In a joint block, all tokens share the same weights, but text, image, and reference tokens each get their own scale, shift, and gate.

In FLUX.1 and FLUX.2, one timestep embedding modulates every token. In FLUX.3, the modulation depends on the kind of token.

The noisy image tokens are modulated by the current timestep t. The text and reference tokens are always modulated by timestep 0, which means "clean, nothing to denoise here". So even a reference that looks almost the same as the output is marked as given context, not as something to generate.

The distilled checkpoint is a flow map. It is also told the timestep each step jumps to. That second timestep gets its own embedding, which is added to every token's modulation, so each of its 16 steps can make a larger jump.

Attention on its own doesn't know where a token is (this phenomenon is called permutation equivariance). RoPE fixes that by rotating each query and key by an amount that depends on the token's position. FLUX.3 uses four position axes, (t, h, w, l) (timestep, height, width, length of sequence), and gives each one a quarter (32 dimensions) of every 128-dimensional attention head:.

It has been revealed that text tokens line up along l, like words in a sentence. The image and the references are 2D grids in (h, w), separated from each other along l. Because a reference uses the same (h, w) coordinates as the output, "the same spot in the reference" has a precise meaning to the model, which is what the src_bbox / tgt_bbox editing relies on.

Recent findings suggest that FLUX.3 is a flow-matching model. Generation starts from pure noise, and at each of the 50 steps the transformer predicts a velocity. This is the direction from noise toward a clean image. The scheduler takes one step along it.

Recent findings suggest that at every step you can also read off the model's current guess of the final image. Decoding that guess at a few steps reveals how the image takes shape:.

Recent findings suggest that the fox, its pose, and the light are already in place by step 10, while the noise level is still 0.97. The snow-laden branches and the texture of the fur only appear in the last few steps. FLUX.3's scheduler uses a large time shift (6.93), which keeps the noise level high for most of the run: 44 of the 50 steps happen above σ = 0.5. We built this figure by adding one small block to the pipeline, which brings us to Modular Diffusers.

If you are fresh to flow matching, we have a beginner friendly tutorial and a video for you to understand how it works.

FLUX.3 ships as a Modular Diffusers pipeline.

You can list the workflows and print the exact blocks of each one, without loading any weights.

Industry observers note that get_workflow() resolves the auto branches and gives you the plain sequence of steps that will run. print(blocks.get_workflow("image_conditioned").doc) prints the components, inputs, defaults, and outputs of that workflow.

Pop the text encoder out, encode the prompt once, free it, and generate from the cached embeddings.

The denoising figure above came from one extra block that records the model's guess of the clean image at every step:.

Amazon VPC Lattice now supports CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (303 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Amazon VPC Lattice now publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources.
  • Recent findings suggest that with these metrics, you can proactively catch connectivity challenges and optimize resource capacity.
  • According to recent reports, cloudWatch metrics for VPC resources are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon VPC Lattice is available.

Amazon VPC Lattice now publishes Amazon CloudWatch metrics for VPC resources. Resource owners — those who share resources via VPC Lattice — and resource consumers — those who access those shared resources — can now see TCP traffic to resources such as databases, clusters, and on-premises endpoints. Resource owners get metrics for resource gateways and resource configurations. Consumers get metrics for resource endpoints, service network endpoints, and service network VPC associations. Previously, resource access logs were the primary way to see this traffic, but they required additional processing and provided limited real-time visibility. Now you can monitor your layer-4 resources directly in CloudWatch.

Recent findings suggest that with these metrics, you can proactively catch connectivity challenges and optimize resource capacity. Capacity planning metrics — including bytes processed, new flows, and active flows — let resource owners monitor traffic per resource gateway and per resource configuration to track load on shared resources. Reliability metrics, such as dropped packets, help you detect problems early. Resource gateways also report port allocation errors, which show when a resource gateway needs more IPv4 addresses per network interface. Consumers can monitor traffic per resource endpoint, service network endpoint, or service network VPC association. They can set CloudWatch alarms for when new flows drop to zero or dropped packets increase, catching an unreachable resource before their applications do. Both owners and consumers can break metrics down by Availability Zone to isolate zonal issues or verify connections after configuration changes.

According to recent reports, cloudWatch metrics for VPC resources are available in all AWS Regions where Amazon VPC Lattice is available. For the list of Regions, see the Amazon VPC Lattice FAQs.

To learn more, see CloudWatch metrics for Amazon VPC Lattice in the Amazon VPC Lattice User Guide, or visit the Amazon VPC Lattice product page.

#20389. Industry News: Amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (266 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Industry News: Amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (266 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback.
  • In a recent development, until now, Route 53 treated an associated private hosted zone as fully authoritative for its domain, so queries for names that weren't in the zone returned NXDOMAIN.
  • To get started, create a private Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing private hosted zone, and then turn on public DNS fallback.

Industry observers note that amazon Route 53 private hosted zones now support public DNS fallback. When a query for a name in your private hosted zone's domain doesn't match a record in the zone, Route 53 returns the answer from public DNS instead of a "name not found" (NXDOMAIN) error. Public DNS fallback is part of the Advanced Hosted Zones offering.

In a recent development, until now, Route 53 treated an associated private hosted zone as fully authoritative for its domain, so queries for names that weren't in the zone returned NXDOMAIN. To resolve a few names privately, customers also had to copy every other record from their public zone into the private hosted zone and keep the two in sync. With public DNS fallback, you add only the names you need privately, and every other name resolves from your existing public DNS. For example, your private hosted zone for example.com points example.com to a private endpoint, while partner.example.com exists only in public DNS. Before, a lookup for partner.example.com returned NXDOMAIN. Now it resolves from public DNS.

To get started, create a private Advanced Hosted Zone or upgrade an existing private hosted zone, and then turn on public DNS fallback. You can use the Route 53 console, API, AWS CLI, AWS SDKs, or AWS CloudFormation.

According to recent reports, public DNS fallback is available in all AWS commercial Regions where Route 53 private hosted zones are available. To learn more, see Enabling public DNS fallback for a private hosted zone in the Route 53 Developer Guide and the Route 53 pricing page.
